speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the duty to table an important petition today, signed by several dozens of Canadians, objecting strongly to the government's intentions to impose the GST on books.
Hope springs eternal with all Canadians that the government will come to its senses and abandon its project to tax reading. These petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reaffirm the historic principles embodied in the tax-free status for the printed word by retaining the zero rate in the GST legislation and regulations.
These petitioners and I would plead with the government to come to its senses and to not tax reading.
Let's do it now.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing order 36, I, too, have the honour and duty to table more petitions from Canadians protesting against the government's intention to tax magazines, books and newspapers through their GST legislation, presently being debated in the Senate. We hope that is as far as the bill will get and that it will be defeated.

Routine Proceedings
The petitioners are from remote areas in Saskatchewan where reading is very important. These petitioners call upon the government to reaffirm the historic principles embodied in the tax-free status for the printed word by retaining the zero rate in the GST legislation and regulations.

Mr. Speaker, today I stand to table petitions signed by residents of Toronto, Ontario against the proposed goods and services tax to be applied to books and magazines.
The petitioners feel that this will make the industry very hard-pressed and that the dissemination of Canadian literature, in particular, to Canadians will be far costlier. It will prevent education and it goes against all principles of democracy and our own principles of educating our own people.
I would ask that the government please reconsider its stand and alter its goods and services tax or, perhaps, not pass it.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for your kindness. I must say I appreciate your smiles of encouragement. As a former journalist, you will agree it is an absolute aberration to tax newspapers or any reading matter, whether we are talking about Canadians with a good education or even worse, Canadians who are trying to learn to read.
I got in touch with people in the Kitchener area, where this petition was circulated, and I spoke to a member of the library committee in Brantford, Ontario, who reminded me that now fines for overdue books would be taxed and explained that this would make the system very complicated. It is already a problem to recover overdue textbooks and books, but if we now have to collect a tax on fines-

Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and duty to rise, in accordance with the relevant standing order, to present a petition from 49 Canadians from across the country.
They feel that after 123 years of Confederation we have had some strange taxes in the country, but this is the first time we have ever contemplated taxing education and culture which are the corner-stones of democracy.
These petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to abolish the GST but, if that is not possible, at least to abolish the GST on reading materials.

Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of presenting a petition containing several dozens of names which were very readily attained by a constituent of mine, Mrs. Margot Downing of Woodstock.

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege and duty pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present this petition signed by people from communities in Saskatchewan such as La Loche and Saskatoon, people from Winnipeg, the Northwest Territories; Yellowknife, Rankin Inlet, and Lake Harbour.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a petition which I would like to present pursuant to Standing Order 36. It is against the taxing of books and urges the government to abandon the GST, at least with regard to books, but preferably to abandon the GST altogether. Why stop there? Let us go all the way.
I am pleased to present this petition in view of the fact that the Minister of Supply and Services is listening attentively and I know that he cares about people who are functionally illiterate and who need to improve their education. He has expressed an interest in that issue in the past and I know, of course, that he will want to associate himself with me and other members of Parliament who want the GST to be removed from books.
As I said, why stop at books? Why not just abandon the GST altogether? It is a lot simpler.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to present a petition. I would like to read it. It is a short petition addressed to the honourable House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled.
The petitioners indicate in the recitals that the Government of Canada has seen fit since Confederation, without hiatus, to apply a zero rate of tax to magazines, books and newspapers and now proposes to include them in the goods and services tax.
The petitioners go on to say that whereas uninhibited dissemination of the printed word as a cornerstone of democracy, culture, education and a literate and productive society will be negatively affected by the GST application, wherefore, the undersigned, your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reaffirm the historic principles embodied in tax-free status for the printed word by retaining the zero rate in the GST legislation and regulations.

Routine Proceedings
Mr. Speaker, I was able to read this because while I was growing up there was no tax on books, there was no tax on reading. Future generations of Canadians might not be able to stand in this House of Commons to read because this government is hell-bent on taxing reading. It ought to be ashamed of itself and it ought to withdraw the GST immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise pursuant to Standing Order 36 and present another petition, giving the earlier intervention of the Minister of Supply and Services. I am particularly pleased to note that this petition contains signatures from Dunrobin, Woodlawn, Kanata and various other community names with which you, Mr. Speaker, will be very familiar.
This petition is based on the fundamental belief that to enjoy one's free participation in a democratic society, access to information, knowledge and understanding are essential, and that the GST is simply another death blow on top of cutting grants to women's organizations to disseminate information and cutting grants to native broadcasting and newspapers to disseminate information.
The zero tax rate on reading is a democratic measure and the petitioners ask the government to return the zero rate to reading materials.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, November 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-88, an act to provide for the membership of Canada in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to participate in this bill. I do want to thank my colleague from Northumberland who, on Friday, when this bill was introduced gave our party's response and our willingness to support the bill in principle.
I notice that the bill was introduced on Friday by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I do not know what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs has to do with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Again this shows the lack of commitment that this government has to many of the proposals put forth in this House.
Although we support this bill in principle, there are many questions that need to be answered before we would consider full and unequivocal support for Canada's participation in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. We have yet to be told who will be making the final decisions, who will be accountable to
Government Orders
the contributing countries, what Canada's role will be in terms of our contribution to the bank, where the money will come from, how this money will fit in with other programs directed at Eastern Europe and whether our contribution will affect our already deficient aid in the Third World.
Yesterday and today we have the Prime Minister of Latvia in Ottawa and tomorrow we will have the President of Lithuania in Ottawa. I am pleased that this time the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs are not afraid to meet these people. They still have not clarified whether they will be meeting these people officially or just as parliamentarians; I hope it is in an official capacity. These countries will be asking if they will be able to benefit from this bank. I notice in the bill in annex "A" the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is listed under recipient countries category "c" but we have no clarification whether the republics will be able to negotiate directly with the bank or will they have to go and negotiate everything through the Supreme Soviet in Moscow? When the world finally wakes up and recognizes that the three Baltic states should be given back their independence which they did have and which was taken away from them illegally, what will be their status in relationship to this bank because this is the kind of assistance that these countries can use.
These questions ought to be answered at the outset of our involvement so that mistakes that have been made are not repeated and changes can be made that would improve the over-all effectiveness of this initiative. We should be fielding questions and inviting comments from organizations and individuals who are already involved in ventures in Eastern Europe or those who at least have some knowledge of the cultural and social differences between east and west. We have those resources right here in Canada and although the Secretary of State keeps referring to Canadians of Eastern European origin in his press releases, we have yet to see any of the input taken seriously.
I should clarify at this point that I am not referring to those officials at External Affairs who carry out the minister's instructions. Considering what they have to deal with, they do an excellent job. I am referring to the vague rhetoric that these people get as directives, rhetoric that they somehow have to translate and finely juggle without additional budgets and without additional personnel into real programs. Where is the commitment?

Government Orders
This is not the first time that Canada has joined an organization simply to get the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs the headlines. Much fanfare surrounded our membership in the Organization of American States. What do we hear about that now? Absolutely nothing. There was no consultation prior to the decision and some nominal moneys were spent on joining. What have we done with our membership? Are we making an impact? Are we making a difference? Are we playing a more effective role in Latin America and the Caribbean since we joined? No we are not. And if we are, we certainly are not hearing about it. Canadians are not hearing about it. We are simply cutting budgets across the board and rendering the department impotent in every area for the sake of a few headlines. I wish this was not the case, but I am afraid if one looks at the confusion that already surrounds the existing programs for development aid for Eastern Europe, it is undeniable that this government is not interested in making a difference.
Look at what we have done to our Official Development Assistance. Not only have we cut back on our prior commitments, but we have imposed on the remaining funds conditions that are starving whole populations.
We impose structural adjustment. We insist they balance their books at the expense of food, shelter and health care. We tell them to modernize, to industrialize and to export. Then we have the audacity to tell them that we do not like what they are doing to the environment and threaten to cut back even more.
We suggest as an afterthought the concept of sustainable development and expect attitudinal and program changes overnight. Maybe we in the west are learning that this type of attitude is not working and that we are at the very heart of the cause of the increased poverty and political instability in these countries.
We cannot afford to make those same mistakes again, but if we look at the mentions made regarding basic human rights and sustainable development, we find only passing reference somewhere in the heart of the text versus being built right into an uncompromisable condition.
I know the presenter of this bill stressed how it would cover sustainable development in all transactions, but why was that not built into the purpose of the bill? Why is it hidden in section 1(7), one little phrase pertaining to sustainable development?
What we need is commitment. As is obvious to each one of us, that requires not only money but foresight, well thought out strategies, and objectives. Most of all we need follow through. How long will this bank be in operation? During its existence, do we envision its role expanding to embrace the co-ordination of the various aid programs?
Recently in this House we debated the future role of the Conference for Security and Co-operation in Europe. We talked about the scope of the conference and how it included, among other things, an economic dimension. How will we avoid a duplication of the role carried out by the CSCE, the OECD, the IMF, and the World Bank?
Maybe the bank should be incorporated with the conference. It would seem that in this way duplication may be avoided. In fact a central forum for discussion and responsibility may clear up some of the confusion caused by other initiatives of other economic institutions.
I cannot help but feel that a streamlined, managed process would be much more effective not only in directing the funds, but in monitoring, evaluating and, if necessary, reconstructing aspects that may prove inefficient.
These types of suggestions should be made at the committee level, before the decision for joining the bank is made. I am sure many members of this House, especially members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade, would make very constructive suggestions.
Ideally those suggestions would then be tabled in a report to the government, which would receive serious consideration and would subsequently be acted upon as we as a country consider joining this bank, but that is of course in a perfect world, especially where this government is concerned.

This government seldom consults with Canadians before making major policy decisions. In the event that it would ask for opinions from the public, it has been purely for political reasons, not paying any heed to the recommendations made.
I would like to conclude by urging the government, at the very least, to commit to this House that forums and round tables will be held on a regular basis so that there can be ongoing discussions to try to put some sense into all the various initiatives that we are involved with in Eastern and central Europe, hopefully with the result that there will be some real benefit from the Canadian contribution to the bank.
As I said, our party supports this bill in principle but, before giving it final passage, we would like many of the questions raised by my colleague from Northumberland on Friday, raised by me, and then raised further by my colleague from Mount Royal to be answered. I hope, unlike yesterday in the debate on Bill C-40 when the minister refused to get off his butt and speak to his own bill, that today the government will stand up and participate in the debate on Bill C-88. If it does not, we should then pull out of all activities in central and Eastern Europe and not make false promises to the people who are trying to get on their feet, people who have changed from communist forms of government to democratic forms of government, people whose economies for 50 years have been downtrodden and now want to make it. They do not want handouts. They want to become self-sufficient.
If the entire western world looks seriously at a proposal such as this bank, I think we can help the economic recovery in the Soviet Union and in central and Eastern Europe come to fruition much more quickly. And who will be the beneficiaries? Every person on this globe.

subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really quite pleased to rise this morning to speak to a very creative and innovative approach to enabling the newly emerging democracies of Europe to flourish and grow. To do so is really in the self-interest of Canada at the same as it expands and expounds on our humanitarian interest in the growth and development of this area.
There is a strong linkage between this bank and Canada's help and Canadian long-term interests with those of the newly emerging democracies to see them succeed and succeed well in the gigantic task of rebuilding toward tomorrow.
One of the things that Canada and these newly emerging democratic societies will have to take into account is that they will have to be able to compete effectively with the newly industrialized countries of the world, particularly Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan.
I have been privileged to be involved at the international level through the interparliamentary union with many of these countries in terms of policy decisions and political, economic, social and cultural developments. Those acronyms have become part of the lexicon of language to those of us who have an interest, not only in Canada but Canada's relationship with the rest of the world, the NEDS and the NICs of the world.
If that language creeps into the remarks I am about to make, I hope it will be quite clear that the NEDS are the newly emerging democratic societies in Europe, not to say that we are not interested in those that are happening in Latin America, Africa, Asia, and the other parts of the world. Of course the NICs are the newly industrialized countries of the world.
I also want to point out that I was particularly privileged to be on a private trip to Germany to visit my son in northern Germany, in Wolfsburg and Brausch-weig, where he works with the Volkswagen people. The day I landed in Germany was the day the wall fell. I can only express my impression of the euphoria in that nation. I happened with my husband to get on a train.


Government Orders
By the way, we should only have such a wonderful train system. If we had not broken down our VIA Rail system, we could all have enjoyed the incredible transportation facilities that linked that country from east to west and north to south. It is true that one may compare quite well the size of that country, but if each one of our districts had that infrastructure we might be better served too.

speechtext: You don't know much. You're cantankerous.

subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Dick, I do not know what portfolio you have, but go and have a cup of coffee and a little sweet sugar. It might help your personality this morning.
I was talking about taking this train with my husband. One of the things that was so personal-and I think it is so important to recognize it-was the impact of the breaking down of that wall.
There was a gentleman sitting beside us who was coming from Zurich, Switzerland. He was quite agitated and quite excited at the same time. He kept saying: "We've got to see where the wire starts, where the wall starts". As we were looking out of the window going north of Frankfurt, we could see that high barbed wire fence. We could see the towers with manpower overlooking these particular parts of the German landscape. Just the sense of the separation of people and families was difficult for me. This was my first trip to Germany and I had some personal problems, but I also had a sense of participation in history unfolding before our eyes.
Tears sprang to this man's eyes as he looked at that frontier. He said: "I am going to go to visit my family in Hamburg. I have had a call from them. I haven't seen them in 40 years". I could sense the emotion of this man.
Then, when I arrived in Brauschweig the following day with my son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren, we went into the centre of town. There were these cars, the Treblinkas I think they call them, little trebs, coming through by the hundreds from this northeast comer. We went to see the border crossing point and could see this huge wall that extended for hundreds and hundreds of yards and then the barbed wire fence that was linking this place. I chatted with the guards on both sides. We could see friendship between the two sides, even though they had been enemies just the day before. It was a very moving experience.
I went back just this past month to revisit for a second trip. There were no rights to cross just outside Wolfsburg. There was nothing in its way. We went to East Berlin, and the shops looked like those of West Berlin. It is true one could see the traces and one could feel that there was tremendous work to be done, but one could also sense that feeling of hope for a people.
It is very important that we use caution and care as we move in this direction. It is a very important role that we have as Canadians, as do other western democracies, to ensure that this is not just a pipe dream, that this is not just an euphoric moment in the history of time, but that we put behind it the substance and the thinking that is required to help these emerging democracies. Life is not easy there.
As I drove through the countryside of East Germany and through the countryside of Hungary, I could see that it was like the 1920s. The infrastructure was not there. The technology was not there. The buildings were ancient and in need of repair. By the way, we can also see that in other parts of the world, that is true, but we are concentrating our efforts and our hopes on implementing those matters which mean so much to us as a nation, as a people, and as written into the Helsinki Accord, with which I will deal in a moment.
This founding of the European Bank of Reconstruction and Development represents a very important step for Canada in terms of its economic support for these newly emerging countries. These kinds of initiatives are very rare in the history of nations and in the history of our world. Some examples are the Marshall Plan after the Second World War, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. We should be proud that Canada is playing a role in solidifying the foundations of freedom and economic opportunity with this bill.

I listened with great care to my colleague from Malpeque the other day. She pointed out that, as a Liberal Party, we have some reservations about the soundness of the over-all government's approach to this new and very challenging region and world economy.
I listened to the member from Parkdale-High Park as he raised some additional issues of concern. The government should pay attention because it is very important. Without question, the principle of support for Bill C-88 has been enunciated quite clearly by these colleagues. This bank will help spur economic opportunity and economic freedom. It goes a long way to renew human and political freedoms in Europe.
One just has to pick up this bill and read the introduction which is set out in the European banks' schedule. It is an agreement to establish the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. It states who the contracting parties are, and I will come to that in a moment.
This bill, developed by the European nations and ourselves, states that we are committed to the fundamental principles of multi-party democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights and market economics. That is very important. Where have we heard that before in a monetary situation and as a banking bottom-line principle? It is very exciting. It is interesting that we are going to be sending our Minister of Finance, rather than the Minister for International Trade to sit on the board representing Canada. That is also a new initiative.
The second paragraph of the Schedule says:
Recalling the Final Act of the Helsinki Conference on Security
and Co-operation in Europe, and in particular its Declaration on
Principles;
There are four baskets in the Helsinki Accord. One of those baskets is significantly, that to deal with human rights. You would not deal with a country unless it respects and upholds individual rights, freedoms and liberty. I think that that is wonderful. To see this in a banking act is quite extraordinary.
Government Orders It goes on to say that:
Welcoming the intent of Central and Eastern European countries to further the practical implementation of multiparty democracy, strengthening democratic institutions, the rule of law and respect for human rights and their willingness to implement reforms in order to evolve towards market-oriented economies;
That means there has to be the kinds of communications and literature that will enable that to happen. I do not think they will be taxed like this government is doing with our literature.
It goes on:
Considering the importance of close and co-ordinated cooperation in order to promote the economic progress of Central and Eastern European countries to help their economies become more internationally competitive and assist them in their reconstruction and development and thus to reduce, where appropriate, any risks related to the financing of their economies;
This is very unique legislation. I am very excited to read this in a banking act.
The shackles of communist rule have been crumbling throughout most of Eastern European. Countries like Canada, who have benefited for more than a century from such freedom should help and support these newly emerging democracies. It is in our long-term interest to continue in this vein.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to be able to speak in favour of seconding reading of Bill C-88 and referring it to a legislative committee.
This bill would ratify Canada's participation as a founding member in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. This legislation raises many important issues and many important questions dealing both with economic policy and foreign policy. Today, I want to deal generally with the economic or financial issues raised by Canada's membership in the bank. I will leave foreign policy questions to other speakers from this side.
I want to say from the outset that we in the Liberal Party strongly support the principle of helping Eastern Europe reconstruct and develop. In this respect, we support the principle in Bill C-88. However, we are not satisfied with the government's approach to explaining to the opposition and to Canadians what this new regional bank will do for Eastern Europe and how it will change Canada's economic policy on this region.
The issue of keeping parliamentarians informed is crucial, because we have a duty to ensure that our approach to helping Eastern Europe is the best and most efficient one possible. The urgency and seriousness of the problems there require nothing less than our best effort. The government's financial situation also requires nothing less than a well thought-out plan.
Certainly, the events which have taken place in central and Eastern Europe over the past year or so have been remarkable. The year 1989 will long be remembered as the year of European revolution. The Berlin Wall crumbled, the Iron Curtain disintegrated, authoritarian governments collapsed, and a new Europe was bom.
New democracies are being created as we speak. These new democracies require new political, social, and of course economic institutions if they are to fulfil the promise held out by those remarkable events of 1989. Canada has a special relationship with the people of this region. We want to see them succeed in their task of building a strong and prosperous Europe.
Government Orders
Eastern Europeans themselves, to be sure, are working hard to realize their vision of a free and prosperous land. Internationally, countries such as Canada have a role to play in helping them to their feet, especially economically.
The Canadian approach has been somewhat scattered with respect to helping Eastern Europe develop and rebuild. With the establishment of this new bank, there will be no fewer than four different sources of Canadian funds flowing into this region: through the bank itself; through the G-24 group of countries; through the G-7 group of countries; and through bilateral programs.
The G-7, as we know, includes not only Canada and the U.S., but also Japan and other major industrialized economies. The G-24, of course, is a larger group and generally includes European, North American, and other countries that belong to the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development.
There are many questions that must be raised about the effectiveness of using such a scattered approach to development funding, such as how do we maintain control and co-ordination of these efforts.
We certainly have a lot of questions about this legislation. We are looking forward to reviewing it when it gets to a legislative committee. I must say that one of the reasons that we have so many questions is the government's apparent reluctance to inform adequately the opposition with respect to the bill. No effort was made on the government side to offer the traditional briefing for opposition members of the legislature. We had to ask for one. There was very little information that we received by way of background notes, and we also had to ask for those.
We understand that the creation of this new bank has occurred very quickly. Just one year ago, it was only an idea. Departments involved have been very busy co-ordinating Canada's participation, but there is really no excuse for not keeping the opposition informed.
As I said earlier, we certainly support the principle of the bill, of helping reconstruct and develop central and Eastern Europe. Nevertheless, we have a number of questions about this legislation. These questions deal with the reasons for creating a new bank specifically for that region and the government's approach to Canada's participation in that institution. I believe that these

Government Orders
questions must be answered, and the best possible approach must be taken by the government because of the tremendous importance that I attach to our efforts in Eastern Europe.
The remarkable events of this region are intensely personal for millions of Canadians who have roots there. Many have ties of language and family. Few other nations possess the web of intense personal connections to Eastern and central Europe which we have in Canada and, to some extent, in my province of Prince Edward Island.
In my riding alone, there are families who come from Poland, Ukraine and Hungary. In fact, one in 10 Canadians have origins in central or Eastern Europe. This gives us a special interest and a special capacity in helping these countries become prosperous and free.
We also have a large social and economic interest in the success of central and Eastern Europe. Canada's prosperity and our peace of mind depends to a large extent on this success. As a trading nation, for example, we are dependent on trade for 30 per cent of our economy. While most of this trade is with the United States, the markets of both Eastern and western Europe will be important to Canada's economic future. The unifying market of western Europe and the vast and untapped markets of Eastern Europe both hold immense economic potential.
This is why I raise many questions about this legislation, not because we oppose the spirit of helping the reconstruction and development of Eastern Europe, but because Parliament has a right to be informed and to debate fully Canada's economic strategy for this region.
The government's share of this new bank is worth about $460 million. Although the government says it will only have to pay about $150 million over five years, Parliament should be aware that we are looking at a potential investment of close to half a billion dollars.
These dollar figures themselves should highlight the importance of getting complete answers to these questions and others that Parliament may wish to raise.
The first question obviously is "Why a new bank"? Before Canada commits itself to participating in a new institution, with an expected bureaucracy of anywhere from 250 to 1,000 employees, dependent on your source, Parliament should ask why existing institutions cannot do the job.
There are several international banks and other financial institutions already established, such as the International Monetary Fund, the European Investment Bank, the Bank for International Settlements and the World Bank, which would seem to serve the purpose given to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development which this legislation is setting up.
The World Bank is actually the short name given to the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, a name which suggests a purpose similar to that of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
I have heard several reasons why this separate bank is required. Some argue that these other international bodies are often dominated too much by the United States, while they note that in this new bank, the United States will only hold 10 per cent.
Some also say that this new European Bank will be able to develop an understanding and expertise with respect to Eastern European banking that no other commercial or outside institution could hope to match.
Finally, the argument is raised that institutions like the International Monetary Fund deal mainly with Third World countries and that their expertise is not really adapted to Eastern Europe.
I would like the government to explain, in the context of a legislative committee, why it thinks a new bank should be started from scratch. I want it to explain why an institution like the European Investment Bank, which is already operating in Europe, could not have a better understanding of the local economy than an institution like this European Bank, which is starting from scratch. As for American influence, the United States will be the largest single shareholder of the new bank. The American government has already played the central role in writing the bank's constitution.


A second question is not just why a new bank, but why a bank at all? In other words, now that Eastern European countries are opening up to private investment, could western companies and financial institutions not help these countries jump-start their economies? It is interesting to note that even before the dramatic effects in this region in 1989, official aid to the region, for example, loans guaranteed by government and government-established institutions had started to decline and the level of loans which were not guaranteed by governments started to increase. We are also seeing increases in the private sector investment in the region. As recently as the beginning of 1988, there were only 165 joint ventures involving western businesses in central and Eastern Europe. By the fall of 1989, there were 2,100. That is a large increase. In 1988, it was 165 joint ventures but in 1989, we had 2,100.
Now that Poland and Hungary have allowed foreign companies to own a majority of the shares in a project they are involved with, the number of joint ventures and private investment should increase.
Clearly, the government must explain to Parliament why some combination of these existing institutions and private investments would not be sufficient to help Eastern Europe before we give them the okay to create another institution with its large bureaucracy.
I would now like to briefly summarize and conclude. Not long ago, we observed Remembrance Day. Canadians could reflect on what is happening now all across Europe. In doing so, they could not help but acknowledge the historic role our war veterans played in making possible what we see today.
I would like to repeat my party's support for the principle of Bill C-88.1 want to emphasize that we in the opposition have a number of important concerns about how the government is going to participate in this new bank. We would like to see these concerns addressed in a legislative committee.
We believe that Canada has a special role to play in Eastern Europe and that our participation is necessary, not only for that region's success but for our country's long-term prosperity as well. I look forward to a thor-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a unique opportunity for me to stand in this House to speak on a very important matter such as the development and reconstruction of central and Eastern Europe. It is for each and every one of us to play a part in seeing something come to reality such as the economic rejuvenation of central and Eastern Europe.
Many of us in our constituencies across this country have people who have come from Eastern and central Europe, namely Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, and Bulgaria. They have come here at various times in our history to contribute much to the multicultural fabric of this country. Of course we have been pleased with the fact that they have brought their unique cultures and their energy to help us build our own country. We have been very fortunate.
I have been very fortunate in London, Ontario to have people from across central and Eastern Europe come who have come to our various communities to help build the country. Yet all of us, over the past number of years, know about the conditions their families and friends have had to put up with in Eastern and central Europe, the kinds of politics they have had to put up with, and the kinds of undemocratic principles that their governments essentially put upon them.
This really is a unique opportunity not only to help our own citizens in this country and their families and friends, but it is a unique opportunity for this country to do essentially what it did for western Europe. It is another opportunity to help, to put out a helping hand to Eastern and central Europe.
Therefore, it is a pleasure for me to stand and support Bill C-88, which will ratify Canada's participation as a founding member in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. With the historic crumbling of the east bloc military alliance and the fall of modem communism in the east central and Eastern European nations, Canada welcomes the creation of a new bank which we hope will finance the transition of Eastern
Government Orders
Europe from communism to capitalism. Now that we have taken down the fences that have divided us for so many decades, we must not turn our backs on our neighbours during this crucial and critical time in their existence.
Economic problems will plague central and Eastern European nations as they struggle to make the transition from a command economy to a totally private economy. This bank will not be the panacea, but it will be the spark toward international co-operation and development for Eastern and central Europe. Each and every person in Eastern and central Europe has gone through many difficult years. The road to recovery and economic prosperity, as we understand it in Canada, will not be an easy one for them. That is why it is essential to see this new financial mechanism in terms of being able to provide support to the governments that have now renounced their political and economic philosophies and to the people who overturned these autocratic and dictatorial regimes, in their efforts toward economic prosperity for themselves and their families. A strong Eastern and central Europe will make for a stronger world and a stronger Canada, because we will do an awful lot of trading and business with people from Eastern and central Europe.
Economic difficulties should not sabotage the historic changes that are currently taking place in central and Eastern Europe. The developed countries of the world are creating a bank that hopefully will act as the catalyst toward the evolution of economic development. Canadians welcome the opportunity to be part of this endeavour to aid central and Eastern Europe.
Bill C-88 is the enabling legislation for Canada's participation in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. The bank will be capitalized, as we understand it, at $12 billion, contributed by 40 countries. Canada would contribute $30 million each year for five years. Even though this is not clear, hopefully the legislative committee, when it has the opportunity to study the bill, will ask some very pointed and direct questions of the government in terms of our true contribution.
That $30 million each year for five years will represent 3.4 per cent of the EBRD's capital base. This will ensure Canada at least a seat on the board of directors of the bank.

Government Orders
The EBRD is really the first major international capitalist institution that includes the Soviet Union as a full member. The bank is the only institution of its kind in which shareholders include governments of both east and west. Therefore it is a unique endeavour by the international community to co-operate in the reconstruction of central and Eastern Europe. Perhaps this may be a model by which the world can deal with other areas of the world in terms of bringing forward economic development and prosperity. It is an important first step toward integrating reform-minded eastern countries into the world economy.
The EBRD will direct investment dollars to the development of private business in those central and Eastern European countries that are reforming their political institutions. Only 40 per cent of the funds available from the bank will be available to government borrowers, as we understand it. This money can be used for the development of infrastructure, such as road, rail, telecommunications, and construction, especially transportation infrastructure necessary to carry their food to the marketplace so that the people of eastern and central Europe have food at the table.
By limiting the amount available to the government planners, the EBRD is trying to avoid the problems that arose in the 1970s when central and Eastern European countries directed their loans to unproductive enterprises that left them crippled with debt. As has been previously mentioned, Hungary and Poland are still struggling under the burden of these debt payments. Poland has the worst debt load, with payments on principal and interest accounting for 88 per cent of that country's exports in 1989.
Given that the debt problem in these countries is serious, it is heartening to see that 40 nations are willing to pool their resources in order to finance the economic changes that are taking place in central and Eastern Europe. I will give one example. Mexico, a country with a significant debt problem of its own, is one of the 40 investing nations that will participate in this European bank.
The goals of Bill C-88 are worth-while ones. However, there are a number of questions and concerns that this government has failed to answer. As members on
this side of the House have tried to point out to this government, it is rather curious that the government has had only one speaker on this bill. It essentially wanted to ram it through the House, without consideration by a legislative committee.
Let us hope that it is not this government's intent to pull the wool over Canadians' eyes with respect to their hard earned tax dollars going into this European bank. Hopefully the government really wants to get on with moving this legislation through in the most expedient way.
However, it is rather curious that the government has not at least answered some of our questions and concerns. As we have previously indicated, this House is in favour of this bill because it has some fundamental principles that we agree with. It is rather curious to see that the government has not tried to help us support it, but in fact it has tried to pull the wool over our eyes and in turn over Canadians' eyes.
The sole function of the bank, as we understand it, is to finance Eastern European countries and their fledgling markets. Canadians accept that such a financial institution will develop a specialized expertise and knowledge of the region which no other commercial bank or financial institution can match.
As my friend from Parkdale-High Park indicated, perhaps we ought to use the unique characteristics of our own country and the contacts of people living here who have bridges in Eastern Europe. In this way we can make sure that the dollars Canadians are contributing to this bank and through that bank to the people will go toward helping the men and women in those countries in terms of their own private economic development or private sector development which will hopefully provide the necessary jobs that eastern and central Europeans will need.
What is not clear is whether the work of the EBRD will be matched by work that has already been undertaken on a bilateral basis and by a number of other financial institutions. I think that point has been made over and over again. There needs to be a discussion as to whether or not we are creating another massive bureaucracy and whether or not we can truly co-operate and co-ordinate our activities in a number of ways to ensure that the dollars in the bureaucracy will not be eaten up by duplication and triplication of function and purpose.

A number of financial agencies are actively involved in lending in the central and Eastern European region, as we know, today. The World Bank plans to lend up to $7.5 billion over the next three years. The International Monetary Fund is prepared to provide $1.5 billion U.S. in loan and stand-by agreements to address the debt problems. The OECD countries have pledged billions of dollars in financial aid to central and Eastern European countries. Therefore, we have a number of questions. Will the EBRD's activities interfere with these efforts in any way? Will the EBRD's activities affect the the amount of aid being made available by these other organizations? Is the EBRD simply a European-run financial institution that will mimic the functions of other international organizations?
These are serious questions which should be answered before Canada commits millions of dollars to this bank. If the government knows the answers to these important questions, why is it operating in a closet and keeping Canadians uninformed about their own investments? Hopefully the legislative committee will give the government and the people an opportunity to look through this window of opportunity in Europe that we all seem to agree is absolutely necessary.
The bank, as we understand it, with the staff of 1,000, will be located in London, England. A full time 23-member board of directors will manage the day-to-day operations of the bank, and will represent the shareholders.
As now planned, salaries paid to the directors and their staff will represent fully 25 per cent of the bank's salaries. Surely we want some definite answers to questions with respect to this area of the bill.
It would be a waste of time and money to create the EBRD if the aid from all 40 nations could just as easily have gone through one of the already existing international financial institutions. Guarantees should exist that the organization's mandate will ensure no duplication of effort.
As I said before, this is a unique instrument and a unique opportunity. Perhaps one could clarify and even use it as a role model in the future.
Canadians want guarantees that the functions of this financial institution will not be identical with any other already existing institutions. In providing this aid to central and eastern European countries, are we taking away much-needed assistance that would have gone to the developing countries.
Government Orders
As you know, Mr. Speaker, while this country talks generosity and caring, this government over the past four or five years has reduced its commitment to the developing countries around the world. Let us hope that the $150 million which has been pledged over the next five years is not going to be taken away from our programs and policies for helping those in the developing world.
Therefore, why is the government not being clear on this issue? We would hope that the government will be forthcoming during the committee hearings and address this important issue also.
Canadians also want to know where this money is coming from. Is this aid being taken at the expense, as I indicated before, of other countries?
Another issue that has not been addressed even though it is in the functions of the bill is sustainable development. I think my friend for Parkdale-High Park has indicated that if we are serious about the environment, if we are serious about the kinds of development dollars that will go to central and Eastern Europe, then surely the idea of sustainable development should be in the purpose of the bill, and not necessarily as No. 7 on the functions of the bill.
Surely we have matured to the point that sustainable development must be key in terms of development. Therefore, it must be made clear that any dollars that this bank will be lending to central and Eastern Europe will support a sustainable environment.
Currently central and Eastern Europe have a number of serious environmental problems. Those problems endanger the health of its own citizens and in fact of other citizens of the world.
Economic development of these countries cannot continue if it will ignore the environmental issues that are currently being addressed internationally. Economic development cannot occur at the expense of good health. Economic development cannot occur at the expense of the environment. Investments and loans should be tired to sustainable development. Hopefully, our person on the board of directors will carry that message strongly and firmly. Mr. Speaker, despite certain clarifications that I am sure will be addressed by the legislative committee, we have a unique opportunity to support the people and the grassroots movements across eastern and central Europe in the countries that in fact brought about the political changes, the changes to the governments of these countries.


Government Orders
The people of eastern and central Europe have suffered for 45 years under undemocratic, dictatorial governments. They need to be shown that the rest of the world is behind what they have done. It is these people who have borne the brunt of political and economic philosophies that have failed miserably over the past 45 years. One only has to witness the long lines to get food for the table of most of these central European countries. One only need look into the eyes of the people who have been deprived of hope, dreams and freedom for years.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to see that the bill addresses and ensures that the contracting parties must be committed to democratic principles, multi-party democracies and human rights and other principles that this country believes in and was built on.
In addition, the bill in purpose and function addresses those certain principles that are absolutely important to the proper and orderly function of this particular bank.
Mr. Speaker, that purpose and those functions talk about sustainable development. I hope it is not merely the small print but really is the philosophy that will be taken seriously by the board of directors of this new bank.
It is important for us to offer that helping hand, not to make these countries and the people yet dependent on another group, but to provide them with the necessary assistance to help them help themselves. If they were denied freedom, hope, and dreams before, let them understand and know that we are there so that they can believe in hope, believe in dreams, and believe in freedom and democracy. This may be one small way of showing we are serious and are with them and are prepared to help and fight with them.

Fourteen per cent of all children under the age of 18 years in Ottawa-Carleton live in poverty without enough money for basic requirements. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
In his announcement last Sunday, the Prime Minister indicated that he intends to set up a special joint committee of the House and Senate to look into changing the formula for amending our Constitution. Just a few weeks previous, the Prime Minister in this House announced the creation of a royal commission, headed by Mr. Spicer, to hear Canadians on the whole area and manner of constitutional change.
Does the Prime Minister's announcement last Sunday about setting up a new special joint committee of the House and the Senate mean that Canadians will not be able to express their views to the Spicer commission on the matter of constitutional amendment and the commission will not be able to consider this aspect of constitutional change? If so, is this not contrary to the spirit in which the Prime Minister spoke in this House when he created the commission headed by Mr. Spicer?

Oral Questions

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Not at
all, Mr. Speaker. In fact, when the Spicer commission was appointed, I think I discussed in the House a number of fundamental questions that I thought the commission would be interested in considering, some of the most fundamental questions of Canadian values and the matters that continue to bind the nation together. They ranged from institutional change which was strongly requested from western Canada to the appropriateness of the existence of a notwithstanding clause in a constitutional document which is designed to protect minority rights. These were fundamental questions that I thought, among others, would be examined by the Spicer commission.
There is nothing at all in that mandate which precludes the possibility of consideration there or opinions expressed there relating to section 38 of the Constitution Act, 1982. But I always felt that it would be appropriate that that problem be given special attention. The idea of appointing a joint Senate-House of Commons committee to consider the matter and to invite participation, criticism, and observations from Canadians across the country surely is consistent with what my hon. friend and, I think, all members want, namely, the greatest degree of public participation in the parliamentary and constitutional process.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The
Prime Minister speaks of public participation. Will he assure this House and the Canadian people that Canadians will be able to appear as witnesses before the special joint committee of the House and Senate that he has proposed and that it will not be another closed-door operation? Furthermore, will he assure this House and the Canadian people that if Canadians are able to appear before the special joint committee and they wish to express their views on constitutional change, in addition to the matter of amending the Constitution and the formula for it, they will not be limited to that narrow question and will be able to express their views on the whole area of constitutional change and development for this country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary committee will be established with a difficult question in mind. For those of us who have been through it, the question of amending a
constitution during the three-year time period raises a great deal of difficulties. This has been expressed by most, if not all, of the participants in constitutional reform over the last seven or eight years.
The object of the exercise is to deal specifically with this very serious problem, but committees of the House can establish their own rules. I know that no one is interested in cutting off anybody's input in regard to improvements to the Constitution or to the parliamentary process.
I understand that the House leader is meeting this afternoon with other House leaders to agree upon its composition and the manner in which it might operate. I am sure that all parliamentarians would welcome the input of Canadians both on this and on other matters.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the procedure for changing the amending formula for our Constitution requires the unanimous consent of all the provinces, how does the Prime Minister intend to go about obtaining this unanimous consent once the joint committee's report is tabled? Furthermore, does the Prime Minister promise to act on this report, in addition to giving it his approval, or is he going to shelve it as he did with the Charest Committee's report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
How, Mr. Speaker? I assume there are several ways to obtain unanimity. In 1987, we obtained unanimity when 10 provincial premiers, the Prime Minister and the three major parties in the House of Commons agreed to support the Meech Lake Accord. So it was practically unanimous.
The problem at the time was not how to obtain unanimity but how to preserve that unanimity over a three-year period, during which provincial governments might change. In fact, new premiers came on the scene and rejected the agreement approved previously by their predecessors. This is a serious dilemna for anyone who wants to see Quebec become part of the Canadian Constitution, on reasonable and honourable terms. Obviously, a different procedure is required. We obtained unanimity on the Meech Lake Accord in 1987. The problem was to preserve it, as changes occurred at the provincial level, and that is what the parliamentary committee will have to deal with.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The new initiative announced by the Prime Minister on the weekend did not, unfortunately, meet with the kind of unanimous support he hoped to see. In some circles there was even a certain amount of scepticism about this new government initiative. I realize the Prime Minister either did not have time or did not think it appropriate to consult the Leader of the Opposition or the Leader of the New Democratic Party on creating this new committee.
However, I would like to know whether he took the time to consult with some of his provincial counterparts, and more specifically, whether he received some indication from the Government of Quebec of its political will and its support for this new initiative by the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our decision was based on a number of recommendations and observations that have been made by provincial premiers and members of this House for quite some time regarding the strictures of Section 38 of the present Constitution. For years, many parties have stressed the paralysis that ensues as a result of implementing this provision.
We had an example quite recently, and I am referring to last June, when we had a quasi-unanimous consent. One of the premiers refused to put the question to a vote before his legislative assembly. Hence the consequences we see today. We must avoid this in future, if at all possible. Because of this concern, which I am sure the hon. member shares, the parliamentary committee will start sitting as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister knows full well that over and above the amendment formula issue there is another basic question in the minds of Canadians from coast to coast, in Quebec, out west or elsewhere in the country: changing the distribution of responsibilities, dealing now with a new distribution of powers between the central government, the provinces, and even the municipalities. That is where the problem lies and I wonder why the Prime Minister would establish a parliamentary commit-
Oral Questions
tee to debate the amending formula when he should strike a parliamentary committee to look into the real, problem, which is the distribution of responsibilities. Why did he not appoint such a committee? Will he not reconsider his decision and make sure that the parliamentary committee tackles the real issue, that is the redistribution of powers between the federal government and the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with my friend that indeed the country has to come to grips with a new and very important question of distribution of responsibilities. I share my friend's point of view. Still we must not lose sight of the fact that hardly a few months ago the five modest and minimal conditions spelled out by Quebec were consid-erd by some Canadian leaders as being much too revolutionary to be acceptable to the central government or to other provinces, and therefore that minimum was rejected at the time.
So we are looking at two issues, one fundamental, the other procedural. First of all we must deal with the procedural matter in the coming days, and I quite agree with my friend that in due time in the not too distant future the Parliament of Canada will have to deal with a much more pressing issue. Those people who barely a few months ago said that the Meech Lake Accord contained overly expensive conditions will now have to re-examine the problem from a different perspective.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister, because this situation is alarming. What will the Prime Minister do to avoid this catastrophy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my friend the Leader of the New Democratic Party raised this issue yesterday, and I would suggest that the statistics I gave concerning the downward trend in poverty in Canada are encouraging. Some 956,000 Canadians have benefitted from government policies and now live above the poverty threshold-333,000 women and 299,000 children. Can we do more? Yes, of course. As far as I am concerned, one Canadian child living in poverty is one too many. Our national commitment should be to do everything we can to make sure that our children grow up in economically sound conditions, and this can be done by eliminating problems associated with poverty.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in agreement with the Prime Minister that there is a need to have a plan to fight poverty in this country and to fight the recession in this country that this government's policies have created.
About a year ago I stood in this House and brought to the attention of the government that it must act immediately on behalf of Canadian farmers who at that time were facing economic devastation. Agriculture Canada has predicted a 25 per cent decline in farm incomes and a staggering 68 per cent decline in Saskatchewan alone.
If we are to attack poverty in this country and if we are to attack the recession in all of the sectors of this economy, will the Prime Minister start by committing his government today to a permanent sensible income support program for farmers, including debt restructuring? In that regard, we have already put in place a plan for the Advance Payment Enhancement Programs and the farmers will receive money very soon.
We also launched two programs, Mr. Speaker: the GRIP and the NISA, that had been more than a year in the making as part of the comprehensive review of agricultural policy.
We had discussions with the provinces and we are about to sign agreements with each of the provinces that have agreed to share with us the long term financing of the programs, for the benefit of the Canadian farmers.
You must realize that agriculture is a divided jurisdiction. By that we mean that the provinces have to do their fair share. Over the past few years, we responded very positively to the farm producers' requests, Mr. Speaker. As we speak, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds are defending the interests of our farm producers in Brussels.

There is a serious question about child poverty in this country. There is a serious question about the fate of farmers, whether we are even going to be able to have food self-sufficiency in this country. There is no question that the recession is deepening. Unemployment rates are predicted to climb to over 9 per cent.
When the Prime Minister looks at the figures which indicate that we could even be in a worse position now than in the Liberal-created recession of 1981-82, what is he going to do? Will he consider establishing an all-party committee to attack the recession in this country and to talk about a real economic plan for this country?

Stop the GST.

What we have going now are some difficult economic times that we are in the process of working our way out of, while maintaining a non-inflationary climate. It is very important that inflation be wrung out of the economy because otherwise, if we followed some of the ideas of my hon. friend, the people who would be most hurt-

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the statement by my hon. friend would come as a very serious surprise to the 40 members of the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology with whom I spent three or four hours last week. They represent the research and development, business and university communities across Canada. They recognize that while Canada does lag behind some of our important competitors in terms of productivity and in some areas of research and development, they indicated at that meeting the remarkable strides that had been made by this government with Centres of Excellence, the Canada scholars program, and the general funding programs since 1984.
Bill C-22, for example, is a classic illustration where $1.3 billion of new investment will go into the pharmaceutical industries in Canada in research and development simply as a result of an important piece of legislation that passed this House and eventually passed the Senate. They indicated to us their desire to work closely with the government and with all parliamentarians to improve Canada's competitiveness. This is an important factor and I know that I can enlist the support of my hon. friend in that very important national objective.

Mr. Speaker, it appears we are making some progress. At least now we are getting the top guns on the other side talking about science and technology. We hope that there will be performance.

Oral Questions

Does this government have in place a program or a plan of action that will correct the situation that this government's monetary policy has caused which is hurting the development of research and development in this country?

Oh, oh.

That concerns all Canadians because it involves our job-creation capacity which is of great importance.
They did point out the fact, and I know my hon. friend would want me to conclude by mentioning this, that in terms of the federal government's fiscal policy, Canada has with the exception of Australia, the most generous fiscal situation for the attraction of investment capital for research and development in Canada.

GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.


Oral Questions
There has been much talk and attention on the current impasse between the European Community and other countries over subsidy proposals in the GATT negotiations. All Canadians are concerned about the implications for Canada should the current impasse continue.
What action is Canada taking to break the current impasse? What are the government's plans should these talks fail?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture called me this morning from Brussels where these talks are ongoing.
He, like a lot of others, is discouraged somewhat by the attitude of the European Community whose position, put on the table again yesterday, does not vary substantially from the disappointing position that it put out with regard to agricultural subsidies some months ago.
Last night, under the leadership of the Swedish minister who is chairing that subcommittee, there were a number of bilaterals in which our Minister of Agriculture is actively involved. We hope that this will break the deadlock of the unfair trade distorting subsidy attitudes that the community has adopted, which then provokes a counterpoint from the United States and places Canadian farmers in very serious jeopardy.
The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture is working very carefully with all of his colleagues from the Cairns group to provoke a new offer from the Europeans which hopefully will get us out of this unacceptable cycle of heavy subsidies with which Canadian farmers and the Canadian treasury cannot realistically compete.

subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard nothing about the discussions concerning supply-management, despite the fact that the European Community and Canada seemed to have a basis for agreement.
The European Community has said that it wants to have a definition of Article XI that would allow countries with production quotas to maintain import controls.
Given the similarity between the European and the Canadian positions on supply-management, what has the Prime Minister done to get his American friends on side?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: GENERAL AGREEMENT ON TARIFFS AND TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Article XI was specifically discussed yesterday in Brussels. The Japanese, the Koreans, the entire Cairns group and most of the world's agricultural traders agreed with the position set forward by Canada in respect of Article XI.
That is the position that the Minister of State for Agriculture and the Minister of Agriculture worked out in intimate consultation with Canadian agricultural producers. This is the one we have been defending around the world, and this is the one that is now achieving a wide degree of acceptance at Brussels.
If we maintain that degree of solidarity, Canada will prevail with its important position.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Shefford rises on a point of order.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
In effect, you are asking the House to proceed to a recorded division under a consent given on December 3rd.
I should like you to look closely at the procedure and the text of this motion which was adopted to the effect that at this time, upon request from the whips of the recognized parties, the result of some divisions would apply to a number of motions, according to the agreement announced by the said whips at this time.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this type of agreement does not reflect at all the reality of the House. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I ask you to look into this very closely.
It may have been possible at a time when the three whips could get together as a privileged few and speak on behalf of ordinary members who, in some cases, were nothing more than voting machines. But this is no longer possible because there are in the House about a dozen members without any authorized whip to represent them.
Therefore, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to look again at the value of motions of this type within the context of the House and its membership as it is now. I refuse to be taken for granted by the whips of those other parties who are not authorized to speak on our behalf.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been consultations with the Whips. There will be ample opportunity for every member of the House to express their opinion on each of the motions. What the Whips have dealt with is the sense of the motion and about how many times we would actually have to collectively stand up.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you have called in the members and that we proceed with that 15-minute bell, at the conclusion of which my colleague across the way from the Official Opposition, will indicate the decision which the Whips are recommending to the House. If an argument must take place, that might be the appropriate time for it. I think we should proceed with calling in the members.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government whip behaves as though he owned the right to vote of all the members of this House and as though the whip of the Official Opposition represented his party and tried to come to an agreement.
Mr. Speaker, what I am asking you to do is to look into the notion that we have to abide by the arbitrary decision of the Whips. Mr. Speaker, it is clear that I would not want to embarrass the House which is about to vote on such an important bill. I know that the Minister of Communication wants to use his time in Canada doing something other than spending his afternoon in the House. The fact is, however, that I feel this type of motion is unacceptable, in view of the current conditions prevailing in this House and I would not want ever again to be bound by such an agreement between three individuals who do not speak on behalf of independent members.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let us not get carried away. Yesterday, in this Chamber, we gave unanimous consent to a procedural order. I will not comment on the attendance of the hon. member, but I know that I was here, Mr. Speaker, and that the House gave its consent, recognizing that there must be some arrangement on the question of voting. The question now is whether or not we should vote, and I think we should. Then, we will have to decide if the vote just held should apply to another one. We will see then, Mr. Speaker, but I remind the hon. member that whips-and I am one of them-are responsible for the orderly conduct of the business of the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just want to bring to the attention of the hon. member for Shefford the fact that the motion last night is totally consistent with the rules and procedures of the House. Perhaps he would want to read citations 78(1), (2), and (3) of our Standing Orders.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I thank the hon. members for their assistance to the Chair. The hon. member for Shefford is complaining.

He is complaining about the motions which, yesterday, received unanimous consent.

The hon. member may not be happy about it, but the fact of the matter is that the House passed the motion unanimously and I am not at all sure that there needs to be any further discussion about it. As a consequence I must proceed.
