speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Pursuant to order made on Monday, December 3,1990, the bill will be read the third time now.
Government Orders
Hon. Marcel Masse (Minister of Communications)
moves:
-That Bill C-40, An Act respecting broadcasting and to amend
certain Acts in relation thereto and in relation to
radiocommunication, be now read a third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I know that I speak for many Canadians in saying that I am both reassured and very pleased to see Bill C-40, a new Broadcasting Act for Canada, receive Third Reading in this House. I know, because many Canadians have written to me from all across the country, urging Government to proceed rapidly with third reading and passage of this bill.
One such letter expressed, in my view both clearly and cogently, the most important reasons why this legislation should become law. The letter read in part and I quote: "Canadians want made-in-Canada programs; we want our special cultural differences and similarities promoted on radio and TV, not submerged; we want more Canadian programs, not fewer, for better choice; we want our Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and our CRTC to be strong and independent, with the public's interests given precedence."
I can think of no better summary of Bill C-49's objectives.
The Canadian broadcasting system is in a period of accelerated change. New technologies, such as high definition television, digital radio, direct broadcast satellites and fiber optics, offer the possibility of an ever-widening range of high quality programming services. Yet, the majority of these services are of foreign origin and the escalating costs of program production make producers think in terms of global rather than local or even national audiences.
Time and time again, and despite the wealth of foreign programming already available to us, Canadians have responded positively to those Canadian programs which are competitive with the best the world has to offer. And such programs are increasing in number and variety.
Canadian broadcasters are realizing that to compete with foreign services, they have to be different. To recapture their Canadian audiences, they have to offer programming of high quality. To quote Michael McCabe, President of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters: "In the one-hundred channel universe, you've got to be good or they'll switch channels".

Government Orders
Broadcasters increasingly are producing distinctively Canadian programs which will hold their audience and which are finding international as well as Canadian markets.
This Bill will encourage public and private broadcasters to continue to produce not only more but better Canadian programs. We believe that this is the most appropriate way to respond to the challenges facing Canadian broadcasting.
But there are other reasons why we need this legislation.
Bill C-40 will replace the outdated legal definitions in the current Broadcasting Act of 1968 with definitions appropriate to current, and hopefully future, realities in the broadcasting system so that the CRTC may regulate all types of broadcasting activities in the public interest without fear of its authority being challenged in the courts.
Technology always has been a driving force in broadcasting, but the only thing that really matters is program content; all the rest is housekeeping. Bill C-40 is the first legislation to fully recognize this truism of broadcasting policy.
The current Broadcasting Act ties the definition of broadcasting to over-the-air transmission, yet today most Canadians receive programming services by cable and satellite. Some of these services are not even directly available over the air and some are available only in return for payment.
Bill C-40 recasts the legal definitions in the Act to focus on the transmission of programs to the public, regardless of the technology used. In this way, the bill establishes an appropriate balance among all the components of the Canadian broadcasting system.
I want to stress, Mr. Speaker, that the new definitions in Bill C-40 are intended to ensure that all Canadian programming services-present or future-will operate under comparable regulations and conditions regardless of the nature of the service or the technology used to transmit their programs to the public.
At the same time, however, the Broadcasting Act must recognize that the same technologies used to transmit broadcast programs are also used to deliver other kinds of services. Broadcasting legislation should not become an intrument for inhibiting the evolution of services which do not properly fall within its scope.
Bill C-40 is about television and radio programming. These activities have traditionally been regulated because they are cultural in nature and they provide a public service essential to the maintenance and enhancement of Canadian identity and cultural sovereignty.
Information-based services such as shopping and real estate services, data base services, home security services and the like are of a different nature. Most are not now regulated. Furthermore, unlike broadcasting, the vast majority of these new services are not of such a high cultural impact.
By dealing with the transmission of programs to the public, rather than on a particular technology, this bill gives the CRTC clear guidance about which activities are to be regulated, such as broadcasting. It also gives the commission the latitude it needs to determine how best to regulate those undertakings which eventually become involved in different types of activity.
The technologies used for broadcasting and telecommunications are converging rapidly. Bill C-40 recognizes this reality and gives the CRTC the powers it needs to regulate broadcasting well into the twenty-first century.
The bill also recognizes that newer technologies allow programming services to encode their signals for distribution to paying suscribers only. For this reason, it provides a right of civil action against theft of encoded signals, a provision which has found support from the cablevision and satellite direct-to-home television industries.
The CRTC has served Canadians well. Under its supervision, the broadcasting system has witnessed extraordinary growth. The commission has tried to ensure that the range and variety of Canadian programming kept pace with this growth. More recently, the commission has taken initiatives to streamline its activities and lighten the regulatory burden.
The CRTC has largely deregulated AM radio, recognizing the particular problems of that important medium; it has introduced new approaches to the regulation of Canadian content on television, and it has launched major reviews of the regulations governing FM radio as well as cable rates. These activities are commendable. Bill C-40 will enable the CRTC to serve Canadians even better. It will encourage the commission to take initiatives and give it more flexibility to find innovative and


creative ways of pursuing the objectives of the Broadcasting Act with a lighter regulatory touch.
Bill C-40 also will change the commission in several ways.
The bill gives to the Governor in Council authority to issue broad policy directions to the CRTC and will establish clearly the Government's role in setting general guidelines for the broadcasting system on broad policy matters.
Additionally, the bill will allow restructuring of the commission, bringing more openness and accessibility to its public hearing process and greater sensitivity to regional needs.
CRTC decision-making will be decentralized so that panels of commissioners appointed to public hearings across Canada will no longer only hear the matters before them, but also reach decisions. Broadcasters and the public attending these hearings will know that the commissioners they address will be those who decide the issues before them. This is in keeping with the basic principles of justice. The Government recognizes, however, that the commission's mandate requires its decisions to reflect country-wide policies and objectives. For this reason, the bill requires that panels of commissioners shall consult with the commission to ensure consistent interpretation of broadcasting policy and regulations.
We believe that decentralized decision-making with mandatory consultation, provides for an appropriate balance between, on the one hand, a more open, accessible and efficient regulatory process and, on the other hand, consistent interpretation of policies by panels of commissioners operating across Canada.
In the same spirit, the establishement of regional offices of the CRTC provided for in this legislation will foster a greater sense that all Canadians have access to the commission and that it is aware of regional issues and concerns.
Through its decisions, the CRTC affects individual Canadians directly. Its regulations and decisions determine the range and even the selection of programming services Canadians can receive and the cost of receiving
Government Orders
those services. Accordingly, we believe that the CRTC should have a regional presence in Canada.
Recently, the former chairman of the commission, Keith Spicer, supported passage of the Bill, saying that, on balance, the result will be very positive. "In practical terms", he said, "C-40 will give the CRTC much stronger and more credible enforcement powers."
Mr. Speaker, I now turn to the centrepiece of Canadian Broadcasting Policy, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. As the national public broadcaster, the CBC, under this bill, will remain a strong and independent voice and the foremost producer of Canadian radio and television programming.
The bill reformulates the CBC's mandate to place greater emphasis on the distinctively Canadian character of CBC programming.

For the first time, this mandate includes specific references to the important role that the CBC has in reflecting Canada, in providing English and French programming services, in meeting the needs of official language minorities, in reflecting Canadian society in all its aspects, in actively contributing to the flow and exchange of cultural expression, and, in all these ways, contributing to a shared Canadian consciousness and identity.
Certain critics have lamented the removal of the phrase "national unity" from the CBC's mandate. Yet, there can be no doubt that the objectives which I have just stated will indeed contribute to Canadian unity. For how can there be unity without the flow and exchange of cultural expression, in English and French, among all the component parts of Canada, as is foreseen by this bill? How can there be unity without a shared awareness of Canadian identity?

Bill C-40 reinterprets the objective of Canadian unity now in the CBC's mandate in terms which are more appropriate to a truly independent public broadcaster.
In considering this issue, Mr. Speaker, an all-party committee of this House unanimoulsy concluded that: "there must be no suggestion in the act that the CBC has any obligation to serve as a propagandist, even for a cause as legitimate as national unity."

Government Orders
I believe that this was and remains the right conclusion. If there is any doubt that an objective to promote "national unity" could be interpreted in a political way, then such wording has no place in the legal mandate of and independent public broadcaster like the CBC.
Most comments, including those of the new president and of the chairman designate of the CBC, concur that the new wording is a significant improvement. As to the CBC's operations and administration, Bill C-40 rationalizes the corporation's management structure, by separating the quite different functions of president and chief executive officer from those of the Chairman of the board of directors. In addition, the bill clarifies the nature of the CBC's accountability to Parliament while, for the first time, stating in law the CBC's journalistic, creative and programming independence.
Among its many other benefits, passage of this bill will allow the chairman designate to assume his long-delayed rightful title and responsibilities at the head of Canada's foremost cultural institution.
Mr. Speaker, I launched the long process that has led to third reading of Bill C-40, with the appointment of the Caplan-Sauvageau Task Force on Broadcasting Policy in May 1985. It was one of the first iniatives I undertook as Minister of Communications. Mr. Speaker, the government has had occasion to say before that Bill C-40 is fundamentally a consensus document. As we prepare to vote on its third reading, this bill has obtained the support of the CRTC, the CBC, most private broadcasters and a wide cross-section of the Canadian public. It is high time that this bill was passed into law.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to what our Minister of Communications had to say. I certainly would hope his introductory remarks would be listened to with a great deal of care and then be analysed.
I will leave that analysis to the people of Canada, to the instruments that are to put into effect this particular bill, and I believe time and history will prove that the words were right. The message was right, but the application of the message is sadly lacking. And so it is
with a sense of sadness that I stand to speak at third reading of this bill.
It is a very important bill. It is a very important instrument and I would, in the time that I have, do a review and an analysis of where we are in the broadcasting industry, the broadcasting services in Canada. The purpose of Bill C-40 was to update the 1968 Broadcasting Act and is essentially identical to Bill C-136 which died on the Order Paper prior to the 1988 federal election.
The legislation had its genesis in the task force on broadcast policy. It had extensive review by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture with hearings across this land. It resulted in four reports containing recommendations for new broadcasting legislation. The committee and the members of that committee listened to the people, and our report reflected the people. We on this side of the House spoke for the interested parties, while from the government benches we heard barely a word; the parliamentary secretary and now, for the first time, a speech by the minister.
While no persons on the government side spoke to or supported this bill, I have been privileged the other way. In fact, I have been more than privileged. I have been well treated by the members of my caucus.
Bill C-40 was introduced for first reading, I would remind this House, on October 11, 1989. It received second reading in December 1989, was studied in legislative committee from January to March, 1990. It was reported to this House on March 20, 1990, and it languished on the Order Paper until October 31 when it was finally called for report stage.
Rumours that were spread by the government about delays, dilatory amendments, filibustering by this side of the House, were unfounded. I would venture to say they were a gross exaggeration, in fact, if not untrue.
The real story of this bill was the reluctance of this government, the reluctance and lack of commitment by its cabinet, and by its members, and opposition by many of the backbench to the contents of this bill. Otherwise why did we have all those zipped lips where no one stood to speak, support, or defend the minister and his bill. I think that was eloquent silence that indicated a lack of support.


The reluctance on the part of the government because of the badly flawed state of this bill is one thing, I would remind the population and the involved and interested parties, many of whom called me and agreed with me when I explained the process, that I should continue the good fight. They recognize, as this House should recognize, and as the public recognizes that the government controls the action in this House, determines the calling of the bills and the procedure of the bills. We, on this side, do not have control of the legislative agenda as much as we would like to do so.
When Bill C-136 died, Liberals had hoped that the new Minister of Communications would have taken time to reshape a new bill and put his own imprint upon that bill. Again, because the government delayed, Bill C-136 came in at the last minute and it died on the Order Paper. We had hoped that when the minister put his own imprint on it, he might fix the major flaws. Not only has he not done that, he has shown absolutely little interest in this bill. He did not speak at second reading. He appeared briefly at legislative committee and never uttered a sound at report stage to defend his bill. He made up for part of that in a very eloquent speech to defend his point of view right now during third reading. That is the only time we have really heard from him in this House.
Liberals are pleased to see the following provisions included in Bill C-40, from Bill C-136: Women, children, cultural minorities, aboriginal peoples and the disabled are specifically mentioned in the legislation and the need to portray more accurately the multicultural and multiracial nature of our society; originators of program signals and their authorized agents, such as cable operators, will be able to take action in the courts against commercial pirates stealing their scrambled signals and thereby stealing intellectual property, creative products, which is so much a key to the well-being and the functioning of this system; provisions making educational broadcasting an integral part of the law.
Liberals are particularly pleased that the government accepted the following Liberal amendments: recognition of community broadcasting as one of the elements of the Canadian broadcasting system, along with the public and the private; mandatory requirement that the Canadian broadcasting system be owned and controlled by Canadians; that the programming of Canadian broadcasters also include children and reflection of the multiracial
Government Orders
nature of Canada, ensuring that television and radio more accurately portray the reality of Canada in its multiracial as well as the multicultural nature.
There are flaws that remain, however. Earlier I presented on behalf of my party a range of substantive amendments which we believe necessary to make this bill the legislative instrument required to meet Canada's needs in the future.
A number of the amendments we proposed in Bill C-40's predecessor bill, C-136, were accepted, and some during legislative committee study of Bill C-40. We appreciate that. Nevertheless, the changes which have been accepted do not address some of the most fundamental concerns which we have raised throughout this debate.
Let me just remind you that the concerns we have about this bill include, in addition to those I wish to concentrate on today, many additional important policy matters. Among them are the following: we do not ensure that federal jurisdiction will not be challenged to the changes in definition section; the need to make provisions for broadcast programming in representative native languages, as well as increased access to post-captioning for the hearing impaired; the urgent requirement to avoid unfair competition and conflicts of interests by incorporating in the law provisions limiting the role of cable television systems to providing programming complementary to that offered by licensed Canadian stations and networks; the act fails to provide obligatory priority for the carriage on cable of public sector broadcasting services in both English and French, including those provided by both federal and provincial-public broadcasters; recognition of the National Film Board in the Broadcast Act, providing electronic window for Canadians to access our Crown corporation National Film Board productions, financed by our taxpayers' money; assurance of managerial freedom for the CBC.
Let me step back for a moment and look a bit more at the bigger picture, focusing on the specifics I wish to address.
In our modem communications age, the role and impact of broadcasting cannot be underscored enough. It impacts everything around us. It is the way most people get their news and information. It is how many of us get much out of our entertainment. It is a source of educational learning and provides support for our multicultural and ethnic diversity.

Government Orders
Of course, with its power to reach instantaneously into millions of homes from coast to coast to coast, if you want to express from Labrador to Victoria, B.C. and up through the great north, Mr. Speaker, we can reach there in a single moment.
Its potential for supporting our sense of shared values and national unity is fundamental to the role of broadcasting, especially in the trying times we find ourselves in today.
Historically, broadcasting has always been recognized as not just another industry like cars or clothing; instead, it is the central vehicle through which Canadians communicate with one another, a major instrument for Canadian creative and artistic expression in the arts and entertainment and an essential means for providing a Canadian perspective in news and information programming.
It is a powerful instrument that defines us among the nations of the world. Broadcasting has been so important because, as has been said so often, we have a very large country. We are geographically very far apart. We have different languages and different cultures. Our economic problems are difficult because our population is relatively small compared to that of our land mass.
We are strung like lights across the borders of this land and do not spread into the interior in very large numbers. We do, therefore, form a very small market and we need one another. We need to know and appreciate one another in spite of these differences and in spite of these distances.
Broadcasting is our powerful link in this respect. News and information programs are indispensable in keeping us open-minded and informed about what is going on here and around the world. Stories, fiction and drama, deal with our past, our emotions, our dreams, our passions, our weaknesses and our strengths as people and as individuals while they form our thoughts and our attitudes toward the future.
Broadcasting is a powerful means of communications, not just with adults but also with children for they spend about 24 hours a week in front of the television screen. After all, children spend more time in front of that little box than in school. I know they often refer to it as the "boob tube".
It may not be as important as all of our universities and our entire school system, but it rivals their impact on time, interest and attitudes of our children. I often wonder what will be the thinking pattern and the appreciation of my grandchildren about their Canadian heritage.
Will they be North Americanized or will they remain proud, strong Canadians, knowing and understanding their roots and moving this country forward? Stories help see behind the appearance that make us different and help us to understand our disparities and our similarities. For children they explain the past, the world around them and stir the imagination for the future.
We also need to have fun together. We need to laugh together. I am not suggesting that we legislate fun or laughter, nor am I suggesting that we can legislate good novels, plays or short stories. We do not have to.
We have much talent in every part of this land and we shine across the globe. Any country, and especially a great democracy like ours, should quite naturally encourage its print or television dramatists and other story tellers. One of the ways of providing that encouragement is to ensure that the private sector broadcasters as well as the cable system and the CBC, the national broadcasting service, have the funds and the economic wherewithal to play their part.
There is also a need these days to call for reconciliation and national unity in Canada. Quite rightly so. Yes, there is a need. I believe broadcasting can be one of the most effective means to help Canadians better appreciate their distinctiveness, their differences, and respect and love all aspects of our daily life; not by preaching and not by keeping all others out, but by telling their stories, showing their talent with sensitivity, with understanding, with its character, and with its particularity. What we need is imagination.
The challenge of broadcasting is it reflecting Canada to Canadians, which we tried to find in this bill, to reshape our Canadian broadcasting system for the 1990s and into the next century. The whole point was to enhance our ability to reflect Canada to Canadians. That is the whole point of a Canadian broadcasting bill. This is


not the North American broadcasting bill; this is the Canadian Broadcasting Act.
The paragraphs of the proposed Broadcasting Act restate the 68 principles which have been enduring and endured: "that the Canadian broadcasting system shall be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada". They newly add that the system should "encourage the development of Canadian expression, providing a wide range of programming that reflects Canadian attitudes, opinions, ideas, values and artistic creativity, displaying Canadian talent in entertainment programming, and offering information and analysis concerning Canada and other countries from a Canadian point of view".
Throughout this bill it is clear that as Canadians we will continue to require, as we have for decades, that broadcasting stations and networks both provide programming that is Canadian in its character and that will be owned and controlled by Canadians.
Where will these nice words really take us? How have the 68 promises been enacted? Unfortunately not in terms of making broadcasting the effective tool for the development of Canadian identity that could have been realized. Some have said that all we had to do was not to develop a new bill and spend millions of dollars in so doing, that all we needed to do was to apply the 1968 Broadcasting Act and tell the instruments that were to apply it that this time we really meant it. We have not done that. While we have been developing this new act, we have diluted certain very important aspects.
Let me tell the House what the 1968 act allowed, because we did not apply its thought and its meaning. The result is that in total a maximum of 4 per cent to 5 per cent of the stories presented to Canadians, jointly on both English and French public and private sector networks, is Canadian. It is only 4 per cent to 5 per cent; no more than one in twenty. Almost 95 per cent of them is American. That is what we see on our television screens; that is what our children see.
I am not suggesting that watching American programs is wrong, not at all. There are just as many-in fact there are more-wonderful, excellent programs being produced across the United States, but there are also poor products. They are often called in the industry schlock. There are poor products on many channels. There are in Canada as well. I do not think our percentage is any worse than that being produced in the United States.
Government Orders
What I am saying is that Canadians watch Canadian productions, but they do not watch them as much because they do not have the selection or the choices they really would like to have. I would say that when we get Canadian products Canadians watch them because they are good. In fact, many do not even realize that they are watching good, solid Canadian productions: Street Legal, E.N.G., Love and Hate, Neon Rider, Max Glick, or the ever popular Degrassi High or The Road to Avonlea. In French-

-Les Dames de Coeur, Lance et compte, Lesfilles de Caleb and many more.

In looking at another aspect with respect to the new technologies, the question is: Who is going to control this system, the technology or the Canadian people? Ownership and programming content are not the only fundamental issues which the new broadcasting bill must address if it is to prove effective in the future.
As the former Minister of Communications pointed out, broadcasting has been changed enormously by evolving technologies since the 1968 Broadcasting Act was passed and will continue to change. Among those technologies are satellites, fibre-optics, cable, and even the VCRs which we all plug in and rent films for. With the arrival of satellite communication and other new technologies, the distinction between different media and the boundaries and frontiers between nations have become blurred. Broadcasting has become global. Europeans are now addressing this issue, both at the Council of Europe and in the new cultural commission which has been established in Brussels, the new capital of Europe. Once it was organized within countries and regulated because of the finite spectrum of wave bands.
Mr. Speaker, as a former broadcaster, I am sure you are aware of and appreciate the dilemma that this technology has presented. The new technologies destroy the rationale for the distinctions we had before with the wave bands. Above all, they make possible the distribution of signals and programming. These new technologies are being built by the few, the sky barons, as the media call them. Through mergers and takeovers they are fighting for control of what the world will see, read, and hear in the coming century. That control includes the creative artists who define and describe the images we will see. The control extends, therefore, to the

Government Orders
imagination of individuals. It affects how we will see ourselves.
Therefore I believe that the content of programming becomes key. As we see technology ever developing and further globalization during the next decade, we will no longer be able to regulate Canadian content on our airwaves. The window of opportunity is very small. If we want to establish a firm and solid base on which to grow in the future, the infrastructure must be in place, and now is not too soon. Canadian programming is going to have to compete, not only with American, but with Australian, British, French, Belgian, and Italian. Subtitling will become part of our normal day. As I said, we must create opportunities so that Canadian programs will be developed and will help define us on the world screen.
Part of the solution lies with the development of the public and private sector, which have important, complementary roles to play in the Canadian feature film industry and in the area of regulation before these sky barons and skypix take over. In addressing the issue of the present and the future of our system, the crucial test will not just be the extent to which the provisions of the 1968 act are retained. The key test will be the extent to which in a more complex situation we continue to retain control by Canadians over the system and to provide a reasonable balance between Canadian and foreign programming.
There are two quite different and quite separate aspects of this issue of foreign versus domestic programming balance. First, what proportion of the programming offered by individual stations or networks should be Canadian? Second, what proportion of the programming offered by distribution undertakings such as cable systems should be Canadian?
This question of how Canadian the programming offered should be was much simpler in the past. The 1968 act provided that each broadcaster should use predominantly Canadian creative and other resources. At that time it was not considered necessary to deal with cable television. Until the early eighties, not so long ago, this provision was interpreted to mean that over half of the programming provided by each station or network
should be Canadian. In light of the lack of clarity in the law and the financial difficulty for some services of providing predominantly Canadian programming, the CRTC allowed a number of such services to operate with more limited levels of Canadian programming.
In response to this situation the standing committee proposed two changes. The first would clarify the meaning of predominantly Canadian so that it would be obvious that it meant 60 per cent or more of the programming provided should be Canadian; not just the channel, but the content of the channel, the programming.
The second proposed change would permit the CRTC to exempt from this requirement specialized, limited audience services for which such a requirement was just not practical. When Bill C-136 was introduced, this recommendation was rejected, and again in Bill C-40. Subsequently, in response to extensive criticism from many quarters including the CRTC, the government amended the clause to reintroduce the concept of predominantly Canadian.
However, the redrafting has been done so badly that it remains unclear whether the intent is that the programming provided by Canadian broadcasters should, unless subject to exemption provisions, be predominantly Canadian programming.
Given the importance of this provision, the bill should not be passed, in my view, without further amendment. If it is not amended to require that programming be predominantly Canadian, there will be no legislative basis for the CRTC to maintain such requirements. This is a very straightforward drafting issue.
If the government indeed agrees that such a requirement is justified, it should have amended the bill to make this clear. Or, tell me: Do you think it is possible that it was fear of American reprisals under section 2005 of the free trade agreement? Was that the reason for fuzzing the issue? I wonder whether I need answer my own question.
Oh, please do.

No, I am going to leave that to all of you. I believe it speaks for itself.
There is little point, however, in maintaining a requirement that most of the programming provided by individual Canadian stations and networks should be Canadian, if at the same time the programming content offered by the cable systems is to be overwhelmingly and increasingly foreign.
Thm on your set, go station by station, count the number of Canadian systems, and then count the number of American outside the three plus one, the national networks of the United States, CBS, NBC, ABC, and PBS. Just count them and see for yourself how the system has been diluted with access to an abundance of independent stations from the U.S.A.
Then look at the content of our Canadian CTV, Global, CBC, as well as some of the independents to see how many of those programs are duplicated on the Canadian channels. Their presence on the Canadian channels are quite welcome. They are important so that we have points of view from other parts of the world. We share in their fun, laughter, et cetera, but there is a reason that they are there. It is important that those channels be heard and seen. They also add to the Canadian programming content funds available for the promotion of Canadian programming. It is an important role. Duplicating that at different hours through other channels and other means is just not a constructive way to ensure Canadian programming.
Today, therefore, it has become evident that the role of cable is equally important as that of the programmers and the broadcasters to the maintenance of a Canadian broadcasting system. Choices on their system make the difference. Their contribution must go beyond human resources, hardware, and the obligation to provide for community channels. Quite properly the expanded choice offered by cable television has been viewed as positive to the extent that it actually made available to Canadians a wider range of programming that they had previously been able to receive only from off-air sources, and often not clearly or not able to receive at all.
Genuine increase in programming variety is clearly a good thing. At the same time, however, to the extent that cable systems were simply bringing in programming already available from Canadian sources, as I said before, and undermining Canadian broadcasters, the way cable has functioned was and is of concern. There are a
Government Orders
number of measures, particularly simultaneous program substitution, that have been enacted to partially offset these negative effects. There has been virtually unanimous agreement that a new act must at last provide the CRTC with a proper legislative basis for regulating cable television.
Indeed, the communications minister has emphasized again and again that a major inadequacy of the 1968 bill was its failure to deal adequately with technology, particularly with cable. Yet the government has, against the unanimous advice of both the 1986 report of the Task Force on Broadcasting Policy and the Standing Committee of Communications and Culture, failed to provide any effective legislative basis for the operation of cable systems in the future.
The simple amendments that we as a party brought forward could have easily remedied this issue, but the government and particularly this minister were too stubborn to admit that they were wrong. That deficiency in the legislation has the potential to completely undermine all other provisions in this important legislation. It is in fact the Achilles heel of the Conservative proposals for this new law. This issue is so fundamental that I want to review the background to it.
After 18 months of extensive research and consultations with the public and the broadcasting industry, the government's $3 million Task Force on Broadcasting Policy reached the following conclusions: that radio and television, public and private, to the extent that foreign broadcasting signals are carried, should complement programming from Canadian sources, any kind of new programs. We recognize that an exception must be made for the at least 17 foreign television signals that are already an established part of the system. In other words, we have grandfathered what exists today. We are not changing that which is available. However, the presence of a particular foreign signal in the system should never be allowed to preclude the development of new Canadian services. Priority must always be given to the development of our own broadcasting services.
In the public hearings which our standing committee held, the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, the CBC and the Canadian producers expressed strong support for the approach the task force had proposed. You, yourself Mr. Speaker, were a member of that committee. The test in the future of whether to permit the importation of any additional foreign service should

Government Orders
be that it actually adds something significant to the mix of programming available to Canadians.
Specifically, the test proposed was that the service should offer programming complementary to that already available from licensed Canadian broadcasters. In response to this recommendation the CRTC has stated that "it agrees generally with this recommendation", while the Canadian Cable Association said that it agreed in principle. To the extent that they expressed concerns, these were related only to the carriage of stations already available off air. In the case of the CRTC, concern was also expressed about including in the new act provisions related to carriage of the foreign television signals in the Canadian broadcasting system.
In our judgment, this issue is at least as important as any other that has been addressed in Bill C-40, and as legislators it is an issue that now must be addressed. I want to emphasize here that the government is not assuming the CRTC will implement this reasonable and necessary policy of protecting our own Canadian broadcasting system. Instead, astonishing as it may seem, the Government of Canada has categorically rejected these policy recommendations, although they were widely perceived to be both moderate and essential to the maintenance of a strong and separate Canadian broadcasting system. Instead, the position the government has taken is that any restriction whatsoever on the entry into Canada of American stations and networks is in principle unacceptable. I call this Americanization of the Canadian broadcasting system.
This position, which is inconsistent with over 50 years of broadcasting policy, is clearly stated in the government's June 1988 response to the fifth, sixth and fifteenth reports of the standing committee. In responding to this recommendation the government has stated that, "The prohibition of foreign radio and television services other than those whose programming is complementary to that available from Canadian sources has not been included in the legislation, since it would unduly restrict Canadians' access to a new range of international broadcasting services". That is to be found at page 90 of the government response in June 1988.
Elsewhere the response states: "The government's policy is not to restrict access to foreign services". That is on page 28.
The government has explicitly rejected proposed amendments which would have implemented the unanimous recommendations of the standing committee.
We on this side of the House are not saying, Mr. Speaker, restrict access. What we are saying is that in our view new channels should add something new as a choice. What will this position mean in the future? It will lay the basis in Canadian law for allowing all American broadcasters to extend their reach into Canada. The result will be to make it far more difficult for Canadian broadcasters to acquire the right to show the best U.S. programming in Canada, even though it costs a heck of a lot less to buy it than it would for us to produce it.
Even when they are able to purchase these programs, it will reduce their ability to earn revenue where they could be found on other channels at other times. There is no exclusivity. There is no protection of their investment and that is grossly unfair.
Revenues from showing foreign programs are now crucial to the successful operation of Canada's private broadcasters. Just speak to CTV, Global, CBC and see what they have to say about this aspect of the lack of exclusivity of their purchases. The resulting loss of revenue will in turn undermine Canadian broadcasters' ability to finance Canadian programming.
The implications of creating a single Canada-U.S. market are obvious already in the film and theatrical business. In that sector there has been a continental market for decades. The Americans have seen us as their back yard. The result is that most of the revenues earned in the Canadian market flow south to finance more American films, while Canada's own film companies lack sufficient resources and, in fact, often lack sufficient window time and space to substantially contribute to financing Canadian films and the ability to distribute and market them effectively.

The same thing will happen in the future if the government carries out its plan to give the U.S. broadcasters almost unrestricted access to the Canadian market.
Why this radical and far-reaching departure from a tradition of building a separate Canadian broadcasting system, a tradition begun in the 1930s by a Conservative government? Why the refusal to provide a sure legislative basis for maintaining and strengthening Canada's own off air broadcasting services, and developing a strong and separate system of Canadian pay and specialty services?
The only answer that can explain this decision by the government is surely that it knows that any new provisions which restrict the entry of American broadcasters into Canada would contravene the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement. I think that is an answer to my colleague from York South-Weston.
That is the key. I did not want to give it away too soon. I wanted people to think about it-if it was not already self-evident.
We have of course already seen evidence in the areas of cultural policy of the way the government is acting since the signing of that free trade agreement. We saw the gutting of the Minister of Communications' original film importations bill, and we have Simon Reisman's public assurance that the revised and eviscerated bill has at least been made consistent with the free trade agreement. That, of course, is why the film legislation will do nothing effective to protect Canadian interests.
We know that the government suppressed an independent consultant's study of the sound recording industry which, in its leaked form, warned of serious consequences for Canadian song writers and performers and the Canadian record industry under the trade agreement. The consequences of a weakened Canadian record industry for Canadian content quotas in radio is obvious, but it is also obvious how wonderful it is for those outside of Canada, for foreign influence.
We have seen the government reject as well the central proposals of its own 1985 task force on film policy related to the use of the Investment Canada Act to strengthen Canadian ownership and control over film distribution.

Indeed, in the book industry, which after all is one of the basic and fundamental sources of material to produce film for VCRs, as well as stage productions for that matter, and where the government had already established a very strong policy in 1985 to strengthen Canadian participation in this vitally important book industry, we saw in the 1988 new American library decision, the abandoning of that essential Baie Comeau policy.
At the present time the government seems to be avoiding making decisions on a number of Investment Canada cases which will again test the 1985 Baie Comeau policy.
Will those decisions now wait until after the election in order to avoid the embarrassment of having a further withdrawal from protecting Canada's cultural sovereignty and identity? There is, of course, further evidence for this interpretation of the government's actions since other new legislative initiatives which might have contravened the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement have also been rejected.
For example, the government refused to include in Bill C-40 any requirement that foreign pay television or specialty services carrying on business through affiliates in Canada should do so through a Canadian entity licensed by the CRTC. I remind members of this House that this unanimous, all-party recommendation of the standing committee was endorsed by the Canadian Cable Television Association as well.
Failure to act on this recommendation will result in two classes of broadcasting networks carrying on business here: one, those which require a licence and must contribute to achieving Canadian programming objectives and those which can extract money from the Canadian market without a licence and with no obligation to contribute to Canadian programming. For them, Canada is strictly a cash cow.
The result will be a growing sense of unfairness and a resulting undermining of the legitimacy of the regulations applied to Canadian services. The result will also be a reduced ability to meet Canadian programming objectives.
It has been our view that anything that has access to our home television set should have been considered by the CRTC and exempted where deemed acceptable, but not necessary to contribute to Canadian broadcasting.

That includes this new alphanumeric channels that we have got that no longer fall under the Broadcast Act.
There is a threat to federal jurisdiction and the national capacity of broadcasting in Canada. The combination of increasing pressure from American broadcasters for access to Canada, and an absolute refusal by the government to include in Bill C-40 any legislative basis whatsoever for limiting their access to Canada is a sure recipe for the rapid erosion of Canada's own broadcasting system.
The government has further weakened Canada's broadcasting system by putting federal jurisdiction over broadcasting at risk and by diluting the national structure of the CRTC. Let us look at this.
Since the 1930s, broadcasting has fallen under federal jurisdiction, reflecting the recognition that this is a prerequisite to maintaining an effective, integrated national broadcasting system. However, Bill C-40 redefines "broadcasting" to include hard wire or closed circuit services hitherto deemed to be under provincial control.
The bill also dictates that broadcasters and cablecas-ters should now have their services separated into programming and non-programming functions, a rejection of existing legal practice which argued that these changes could only lead to a questioning self-inflicted vulnerability.
Furthermore, Bill C-40 provides the foundation for an argument that a cable company may be subject to two regulatory regimes: one in accordance with which its broadcasting business is regulated, and another, possibly a provincial one in accordance with obligations to maintain different sets of books for different regulators, perhaps using different accounting practices, depreciation methods and cost separation techniques. This is all very costly, and add to that the GST, retransmission payments, and many other aspects and see what is happening in this field.
Second, with the passage of Bill C-40, all full-time CRTC commissioners, now known as the executive committee, will no longer be required for the taking of its decisions. This approach was known as collegial decision making and has been replaced with a concept that is called "who hears decides" whereby panels of three will be empowered to make decisions binding on the entire commission. The introduction of those who
hear decide-Mr. Speaker, did you want me to finish this?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   ENVIRONMENT AUDITOR GENERAL PROPOSAL FOR ESTABLISHMENT
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   ENVIRONMENT AUDITOR GENERAL PROPOSAL FOR ESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing the position of Environmental Auditor General, whose purpose would be to conduct an audit of all government operations on a rotational basis to ensure that any activity, program or initiative of the government is conducted in a manner that is compatible with a policy of protection and enhancement of the environment.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to move this motion today on an idea whose time has truly come.
The concept of introducing environmental audit as an integral part of government operations and decision making has been promoted and supported by, among others, the minister in introducing the discussion paper on the Green Plan, the consultation on the discussion paper, the Standing Committee on Environment unanimously, the C. D. Howe Institute, the Rawson Academy of Aquatic Science, the National Round Thble on the Environment and the Economy, and the Auditor General.
Like value for money or operational audit, environmental audit is an indispensable tool for management control of spending, for the effectiveness of the use of public resources, and for decision making. In addition,

accountability to Parliament and to the public on environmental matters simply cannot be carried out or ensured without environmental audit.
In times of tight budgets and rising public debt, environmental audit presents opportunities for substantial savings on government operating costs. As a new field of knowledge, environmental audit methodology has the potential to be a major international market opportunity for Canadian expertise and knowledge. As well, this initiative by government will ensure that businesses seeking to be more environmentally responsible and more competitive and productive in a global economy will have the tools they need to reach these objectives.
This year for the first time the Auditor General chose to address the question of environmental audit in the first chapter of his 1990 annual report to Parliament. The chapter is entitled: "Matters of Special Importance and Interest". In that chapter, on page 23, the Auditor General talks about "the protection of the natural environment, a prime example of the need for accountability". Ele talks about the responsibilities for protection of our natural environment as being major and shared, and that accountability for them should be exacted.
Section 1.46 states:
One can look at the environment as a fund: a fund of paramount importance to all. It is shrinking while the number of people who must share it is growing. The share of each person, especially those coming after us, is being reduced-for practical purposes it is governments that have been given the operating responsibility (for the environment)-
The federal government deals with national concerns for the environment-Parliament should expect governments to devise acceptable means of being held accountable for the conduct of its environmental responsibilities-
Here then is a case where government's accountability for-the total government effort on the environment-is more important than focusing on the individual performance of departments-
On the question of the environment, the Auditor General finishes up by asking, in terms of responsibility for Canada's environmental well-being: "Who is minding the store?" That is the purpose of this motion today.
I want to make a few other references and indicate to the House why I say that this is an idea whose time has come.
Private Members' Business
It was in late 1970, that the Securities and Exchange Commission in the United States first asked for disclosure to investors of present and future costs of complying with environmental regulations. That was when companies had to begin doing environmental audits.
In 1986, New Zealand introduced the position of parliamentary commissioner for the environment, one of whose main functions is the audit and surveillance of government operations for their impact on the environment and holding government accountable for those operations.
In 1988, the enforcement and compliance policy accompanying the Canadian Environmental Protection Act recognized the effectiveness of environmental audit as a management tool for companies and government agencies.
In the spring, the discussion paper on the Green Plan stated with regard to about environmental audit that the objective "to make Canada by the year 2000, the industrial world's most environmentally friendly country" can be achieved if we lead by example. "As the largest single business in Canada, the government has important responsibilities related to the environmental impact of its own decisions. Good environmental management will increasingly make good business sense." It went on to state that "a number of businesses have already developed environmental audit procedures and put the question, should businesses and governments be required to perform environmental audits?"
The answer from the consultations on the green plan discussion paper was a resounding yes. The August report recommends that all government departments be required to undertake annual environmental audits and make the results public, which is exactly what this motion is proposing.
Those businesses, environmental organizations, and ordinary citizens with whom the government consulted again suggested that "all government departments should be required to conduct annual environmental audits and that the government should develop a code of environmental stewardship to govern the operations of all federal departments". The trend continues from there.


Private Members' Business
The C. D. Howe Institute, in its July publication, talked about the need for good information and cost benefit analysis for decision making to integrate economic and environmental considerations.
We had the Eco Source magazine in August, 1990, calling "the environmental audit the road map to a greener corporation". For the largest corporations in the country, environmental audit is fast becoming a senior management issue and that "companies are realizing they have to factor the environment into business operations. You'd have to be dumb to be in business in North America today and not be taking on these issues."
The certified general accountants' magazine similarly described the importance of environmental audit as an idea whose time has come. It stated that the "International Chamber of Commerce and various industry associations in Canada are exploring how they can best assist their members in the use of environmental audits."
Finally, in October, 1990, the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy, with the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Finance both present and not dissenting, recommended to government that an environmental auditor should be named. I emphasize again, Mr. Speaker, both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of the Environment were present at that meeting when that recommendation was adopted.
The Rawson Academy on Aquatic Sciences, when it was before the environment committee on Bill C-78 on November 8 of this year, talked in very serious terms about the need for environmental audit, pointing out that such an office would be responsible for monitoring the performance of government agencies and departments according to designated standards of environmental protection or resource conservation.
Most of the sources I have quoted have been within the last year. There is an obvious ground swell of support for the recognition that, to truly integrate environmental decision making and economic decision making, environmental audit is an essential tool.
I will refer to only one last source and that is the interim report of the Standing Committee on Environment. The report is entitled: No time to Lose-The
Challenge of Global Warming. Recommendation 16 states that "the committee recommends that the Auditor General, working in conjunction with the Departments of Environment and Finance, establish an environmental audit function to ensure that all federal departments and agencies have implemented environmental assessment processes and to monitor the effectiveness of environmental programs".
Recommendation 17 states that "the committee recommends that all federal departments and agencies, as part of their budget submissions, report on the direct and indirect impacts of their operations on global warming and set annual targets for reductions".
These things cannot happen without the tools to let them happen. As the single-largest employer in the country, government must set the example. The green task force on the Hill, the Greening of the Hill, has been a symbol and a beacon to Canadians that we, as parliamentarians, are serious about our concerns for the environment and are determined to examine our own environment and to make it as friendly towards the survival of life on this planet as we possibly can. Canadians expect the same thing throughout government.
We cannot sit here and decide that we will impose regulations, laws, green taxes, and horrendous reporting requirements on everybody else in the country, and then exempt ourselves from what we require others to do at some cost to them.
However, I do want to point out that a number of sources have told us that what we are looking at here in environmental audit is not an expense, but a significant opportunity for cost-savings. I will give just one indicator. The DPA report estimated that in energy conservation alone, this country could save $150 billion.
Again, I quote from Eco Source magazine. "The new audit is a matter of performance. It examines the environmental details not normally of concern to engineers and lawyers, such as the lighting system, the heating system, recycling practices, purchasing habits, packaging systems, supplier and investment policies. The auditors check washrooms and cafeterias, interview groundskeepers and cleaning staff, and discuss packaging alternatives, employee car poolings, staff training programs, and codes of conduct."


In this government, we do not even know how much we spend on vehicles every year, how much we spend on gasoline, how much we spend on electricity, how much we spend on heating our buildings, how much we spend to have garbage carted away, and how much unnecessary money we spend on paper. We have no system of accounting for those things.
The Green Plan consultations talked about the importance of investing in technology. What better way than for the government, as the largest corporation in the country, to start looking at its own operations, getting its own house in order, looking at what technologies it needs to do that, and then being in the forefront of developing those technologies? Just as a customer for new products, the government has the opportunity to influence the marketplace in a positive way rather than imposing requirements and to ensure that the kinds of products and services that are developed will not only make government but the private sector more environmentally friendly.
Many companies want to be environmentally friendly, but especially the small ones need the tools to do it. Environmental audit in government can help those tools be developed.
I want to talk about environmental audit as a major international opportunity for Canada. As I said, in 1986 the government of New Zealand was the first, and is still the only country in the world, to establish environmental audit in its parliament. I want to quote again from Eco Source where it says:
No government standards exist anywhere in the world for
environmental audit.
It also says there are real commercial advantages in turning out a better than average environmental performance. Finally, it says that "the implications of a full-blown greening commitment on the part of a major multinational or government agency would be impressive, primarily for its ripple effect".
We have in Canada some of the best raw talent to develop the methodologies and techniques of environmental audit anywhere in the world. When New Zealand set up its audit function, it did so with the help of Canadian officials. We need to put that talent to work, develop skills and knowledge that will give us a major product to market internationally, to help other coun-
Private Members' Business
tries and private sector operations become as environmentally friendly as they can.
That is why I say to get into environmental audit is a major business opportunity for Canada.
I want to conclude by saying that we have been trying to tell households, individuals and companies how to be more environmentally friendly, how to cut down their use of energy, how to cut down their production of garbage. Now we are looking at regulations, legislation and green taxes. Why not lead by example?
In the 1970s we were forced into energy conservation, and now again in the 1990s the Minister of Energy is telling Canadians to cut back on the use of energy. What have we done in government to demonstrate how that can be done? The major need now is to do it in business, in industrial operations, not in households.
Certainly the idea of an environmental auditor as such needs more exploration. There are many options as to how environmental audit can be started and carried on. The establishment of a specific position may or may not be the best way to do it. But until we take the first step along the road to ensuring that every government department has the skills, the tools, the knowledge and the necessity to monitor its environmental impacts, we will not get anywhere. We will never decide how best to do it. We will never develop those tools of knowledge that our companies, our private sector, and the public sector at all levels of government need.
Next week the green plan will be tabled. I hope it will not ignore the advice it got from over $6 million worth of consultation. I will only point out that for less than half that amount, the office of an environmental auditor general could have been established.
I hope the government will include environmental audit in its Green Plan to be tabled next week. I would hope that if it intends to do so, it will make a point of allowing this motion to go to committee. All that needs to happen for this motion to receive further discussion and for us to start along that long road to being environmentally responsible as a government, as a Parliament, as a nation, is for government members not to continue talking until six o'clock.
If this debate ends before six o'clock, this motion can then be examined and acted on by a committee. We will have taken one important step down the road.

Private Members' Business
I ask members opposite who are going to speak on this bill to give serious consideration to speaking very briefly, allowing the debate to terminate before six o'clock and allowing this motion to go before a committee for study.

Mr. Speaker, although I am not a member opposite in a geographic sense, I would have to say that I probably will be deemed to be a member opposite when I am finished speaking to this motion.
First of all, I congratulate the hon. member for putting her motion. I have the privilege to serve with her on the environment committee of the House of Commons where she makes a major contribution. Generally speaking, we and other members of that committee are in consensus not only about the importance of the environment to Canada and to the world, but also about the measures that we must take to enhance and protect our environment in this country.
I would have to say that, in reading the hon. member's motion to appoint an environmental auditor general, I believe as well intentioned as her resolution may be, in my view it goes in the wrong direction to the ultimate resolution of sustainable development in the sense that sustainable development means the reconciliation of both economic and environmental factors.
To isolate an auditor general strictly in an environmental sense is to miss the point that we cannot ignore the environmental without considering the economic and vice versa. In fact, I would refer the hon. member to a resolution in which she shared in our interim report on global warming, which was published just before the Geneva convention when, in recommendation 16, the environment committee said that we recommended the auditor general-

speechtext: I said that.

speechtext:
Did you? I missed that.
Perhaps it is worth reading again, because frankly it underlines the weakness in the concept of an environmental auditor general.
It does recommend an auditor general who works in conjunction with both the departments of environment and finance to establish an environmental audit function. I do not think there can be any dispute about the need and the concept for an audit of environmental considerations, as is the case for an audit of economic considerations.
Again, I say that in the concept of sustainable development, the two very much go together.
I would also like to say that one of the areas that has been of concern to the environment committee and to another committee on which I sit, the forestry and fisheries committee, is the organization of environment departments themselves whether they are operating departments, regulatory departments or policy departments.
I think a general consensus has developed and is recommended in this report by the environment committee and also by the forestry subcommittee, that environment departments generally be policy and regulatory departments whose disciplines and policies permeate the operating decisions and criteria of all government departments wherever they may fall, be they provincial environment departments and other provincial departments, or federal government departments and the federal environment department.
The concept of environmental administration should be approached in very much the same manner that economic and financial considerations are approached in a policy and regulatory sense, and not in an operating sense.
I would like to refer to the forestry report in brief, if I may, because this report which addresses the federal role in the forests of Canada is very much an environmental document. It touches on the commercial importance of forestry, but it also underlines the fact that the forests are the essence of the environment of this country. It expresses concerns, as I have said, that environmental policies and disciplines should permeate every operating entity and every operating decision, just as do financial and economic considerations. But it also underlines the fact that operating agencies should conduct the operations.
There is an area of concern that I would like to mention in respect of the initiatives we are taking to enhance our environmental disciplines in Canada, specifically with respect to Bill C-78, which is itself a move in a direction of more intensive environmental audit. I have expressed a concern publicly in the environment committee, and I would like to express the concern again here today that the Department of the Environment, in its environmental assessment review process, does not become a master operator, a font of wisdom in all directions and in all disciplines.


I think it is extremely important that while the environment assessment review process addresses the environment broadly, those disciplines which are affected, such as forestry, fisheries, mining, energy or agriculture very clearly have a statutory obligation and a statutory right to be involved in the environmental assessment process, whatever direction it may take at any given time.
This government addressed the need originally for environmental assessment review guidelines with Bill C-78, to enhance those disciplines, to make not only the initiating minister responsible for environmental assessment of departmental actions, in whatever department they may occur, but also giving the environment minister the authority to oversee and overrule the environmental planning of specific initiatives.
The government has placed a great cloak of security around the environmental process in this country and I applaud it and support it while expressing the caveat that it contain very clear and mandatory provisions for the operating entities, professions and disciplines to be involved in their specific areas of activity.
Another area where this government has made significant progress and, as the hon. member has mentioned will make an announcement next Tuesday, is in the area of Canada's Green Plan. It was on March 29, 1990, that the Government of Canada released the framework for discussion on the environment which began the process of the Green Plan, called "Our National Challenge". Its long-term objective was stated to be to make Canada the industrial world's most environmentally friendly country by the year 2000. There is a lot of evidence that we are making progress in that direction. It was to do that by ensuring that the activities of business, individuals, communities and governments are consistent with the concept of sustainable development. I believe that it has done that.
Canadians responded to the government's invitation to that discussion and, during the first phase, more than 6,000 people attended 41 information sessions held across the country. They asked questions, expressed concerns and they identified needs for action. In phase two, more than 3,500 people participated in two-day consultation workshops, in 17 capital cities and major
Private Members' Business
centres in the provinces and the territories. I participated in one of those in Fredericton and I want to tell you that it was a good consultation. It was the kind of dialogue that gave you confidence that this government really is in touch with the people.
I believe that when we see the green plan unveiled next week, it will reveal that that, in fact, is what has happened, that there has been close, intensive dialogue, there has been effective consultation, and we shall have a national environmental plan, a green plan that will truly address the needs, the aspirations, the goals and objectives of all Canadians. Mr. Speaker, that is consistent with the undertakings and the obligations of this government.
