Mr. Speaker, I would have preferred to defer to my colleague because he is so learned and eloquent on the matters of broadcasting, being a former broadcaster, if one can ever be a former broadcaster, for that matter.
Government Orders
In relation to Bill C-40, I have three major concerns with this new broadcasting legislation. There is no legislative base because the amendments were defeated in three areas: the CBC northern services, no legislation or amendment for the use of aboriginal languages although there is reference in the text of the Broadcasting Act to it, and no legislation for CBC's contribution to the development of national unity. I find that quite sad and quite a sorry statement for the institution of national unity.
I would like to establish a case for there being an amendment with reference to CBC northern services. I cannot understand why there is no legislation for the CBC northern services. CBC northern services are responsible for CBC services throughout Yukon, Northwest Territories, and northern Quebec, over one-quarter of the land mass of Canada. What does that include in the Northwest Territories? Most communities in the N.W.T. receive both radio and television service. Anti D satellite capacity is leased by the CBC to cany radio and television signals for the Northwest Territories. Through CBC's accelerated coverage program, all communities with a population of over 500 now have a satellite receiving dish and low-level transmitter. Similar equipment is supplied to communities of under 500 through the Government of the Northwest Territories Department of Culture and Communications.
The CBC operates four radio production stations in the Northwest Territories. Programming is produced in Yellowknife for the Mackenzie region, Inuvik for the Mackenzie Delta, Iqaluit for Baffin Island and Eastern Arctic, and Rankin Inlet for the Keewatin.
Yellowknife, Inuvik, and Iqaluit produce daily northern newscasts and current affairs programs in English and a variety of northern aboriginal languages. General programming is a mix of northern and national production. The CBC access policy provides equipment, training, and access to CBC radio transmitters to allow remote communities to turn off CBC and substitute their own programming.
Some 30 community radio services are in operation. There is one commercial AM radio station in the Northwest Territories, in Yellowknife. A commercial cable television company also operates in Yellowknife with 10 channels supplied to subscribe to through satellite. Local programming is produced and pay television is available in Hay River, Fort Smith, Iqaluit, Inuvik who also have cable television. CBC television has northern production studios in Yellowknife, and national programming is uplinked from Toronto on two channels. Inuit Broadcasting Corporation with production studios in Iqaluit has been given access to the eastern Arctic,


Government Orders
Keewatin channel at various times during the week. Some programs are simultaneously broadcasted in English and northern native languages through the use of CBC Radio.
In the spring of 1981, native organizations in the western N.W.T. received CRTC approval to broadcast through the Cancom system. The Native Communication Society of the western Arctic in Yellowknife subsequently developed a training program for native people interested in radio and television. They now have a full-scale operational radio studio and full day broadcast, including three hours in live programming with the news and aboriginal programming.
Inuvialuit Communication Society in the Inuvik region established in 1983, has the television production studio in Inuvik and has broadcast through the CBC network since 1985.
With all this, the government does not believe legislation is required. This is very confusing for many people, with the amount of activity and the amount of resources that have been expended to train people to deliver programs in a very challenging field, the field of aboriginal languages. Even developing the terminology to accommodate modem concepts is being denied the opportunity to flourish.
My specific concern with regard to national unity is best expressed by one of my constituents who on July 24, 1989 wrote a letter to the Prime Minister. She wrote: "I am writing to protest the budget cuts to the CBC contained in your government's Budget". Even at that time, that was a concern. She said that the CBC plays an essential role in maintaining Canada's identity as a separate nation from the United States and that this role would become even more important as free trade erodes our identity as Canadians. "Please reconsider your intent to slash the CBC's funding and ensure the CBC receives the resources required to continue to act as a strong, cultural unifying force for Canada." This was put forward by one of my constituents.
I have received numerous concerns from my constituents, one of whom is a broadcaster and a person who works in the field of broadcasting. He takes much exception to the whole idea of privatization of CBC. This constituent is not only a broadcaster, but also an artist and has had the opportunity to express some northern interpretations of his artistic endeavours through a recording by CBC.
So have other renowned northern artists such as Charlie Panagoniak. There are many other young artists who I can think of from the communities who have had the opportunity to produce records and to express in their aboriginal languages the very essence of who they are in the songs and in the music of their people.
We have had numerous applications that have been put forward to numerous sources for moneys to produce recordings of Inuit music or Dene music that express the cultures of the north. These are the kinds of things that were supported by CBC. Many of the people who are trained and dedicated to the whole idea of broadcasting for the north are fearful if in fact there are cuts. I know that it is being denied across the way by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications that in fact there will not be those kinds of cuts.
Well, it is very good to hear because for many of the people who are trained and dedicated to working for the northern broadcasting service it is more than just a job for them. It is a labour of love. It is something they believe in and something they are veiy studied in. It is a commitment on their part to bring to southern Canada and to bring to northerners, not just news and information from the south but from the whole world. It is also a commitment to bring knowledge from the various parts of the north.
When we speak about the north, we are at the stage in development of the north that is very important. I guess we are on the brink of our true constitutional development, where northerners will take their true place in Confederation. There is lots of talk about many issues that are important to the north.
Who brings to the north the importance of what happens at the national level or what happens in the Persian Gulf? It is CBC. Usually it is CBC television and CBC radio. Who brings to the north the importance of what happens in one region? In Nunavut, it brings the news of what is happening with the land claims in the eastern Arctic to the west. Who brings the news from the west to the east? It is CBC. It has always been so.

In years gone by we have had limited capacity. We relied heavily on radio. Now we have CBC television broadcasting. Many of the communities get Newsworld. It has been a plus for northerners who do not have the opportunity to get out into mainstream Canadian society by way of travel, because it is very isolated and very remote. We have the opportunity through CBC to share with the rest of Canada what the north is all about and also to get the message to the north of what Canada is all about, in all parts of the country.
Mr. Speaker!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say just a very few words in connection with Bill C-40, as it proceeds on third reading to final passage and on to the Senate.
You may not recall it, Mr. Speaker, because as I recall you were not with us during the last Parliament. However, all of your associates in the chair will recall very well the fact that during the last Parliament a very similar bill was put forward by the government with many similar provisions relating to broadcasting. That bill proceeded through the House, was finally passed by the House, went on to the Senate, and then, when the election of 1988 was called, it died because it had not been passed by the Senate prior to the election call.
That bill contained some provisions which caused some great concern to a good many constituents of mine, particularly residents of condominiums. They felt that the provisions of that former bill-and I must say that I agree with them-were discriminatory with respect to condominium owners because of the fact that they were treated differently than those who were the owners of single family detached dwellings. In fact they opposed that bill quite vehemently. They presented their views on many occasion, sometimes by letter, sometimes by telephone calls, and ultimately by representations before the
Government Orders
legislative committee that considered that bill, asking for amendments that would have placed condominium owners in the same position as those who were single family detached home owners.
Mr. Speaker, others who sat in the chair that you are sitting in at the present time,will recall that I took a very strong position on behalf of my constituents at that time. I too put forward amendments to that bill in an effort to try to bring about some changes which would put condominium owners on an equal footing with those in single family homes, to the extent that when that bill was at report stage and notwithstanding the fact that I was a strong supporter of the government and continue to be, I did not vote for the bill at report stage. Today we have a brand new bill before us but it has provisions which are very, very similar to the provisions contained in the previous bill that was presented before the Thirty-third Parliament.
I have a great many constituents who are very supportive of this particular bill. In fact, they have written urging me to support it. I have received some 18 letters with respect to this bill from people who are my constituents and who are also members of an association which you are familiar with, Mr. Speaker, known as the Friends of the CBC. Understandably, they want to see this bill passed because it has been a long time since we have had new legislation governing either the CBC or broadcasting in this country.
The previous Minister of Communications in the last government brought the bill forward because it had been years and years since we had had legislation to catch up with the many technological changes, if nothing else, that had occurred in broadcasting since the passage of the last legislation with respect to broadcasting.
Notwithstanding the support that this bill receives and the understandable feelings that we need new legislation, I still truly believe that the owners of condominiums have a legitimate concern with this bill, as they had with the last bill, concerning the impact of satellite receivers. With the prior bill and with this bill, condominium owners feel it is discriminatory and that they are not treated the same way as single family home owners.


Government Orders
If they are regulated under this legislation, they will have no alternative but to become captive receivers and captive subscribers to cable television, whereas the single family home owner is not in that position. If the single family home owner was regulated, he or she could very well drop the subscription to cable television, set up a satellite receiver in their own backyard and have no problems whatsoever.
Very kindly, the parliamentary secretary in his remarks this evening has pointed out that there is some protection, if not in the legislation, at least in the hearts of the government, the minister, the parliamentary secretary and the department for the condominium owners in this situation. I have no reason to doubt the words of the parliamentary secretary. I applaud his words and I thank him for them.
However, you and I know that he will not always be the parliamentary secretary, the present minister will not always be the minister and the present government will not always be the government. With great respect, I fully understand that with a democratic system, Mr. Speaker, from time to time-it may be a long time and, hopefully, as far as you and I are concerned, it will be a long time-one of these days there will be another government, another minister, another parliamentary secretary and who knows what their views may be.
And so tonight, while I speak in support of the bill, I want to voice my concerns and the concerns of my constituents who are condominium owners, and there are a great many of them. I want to point out as well with respect to the bill in the Thirty-third Parliament, there were some 266 individual residents of my riding who voiced personal concerns about that bill.
With respect to this bill, some 158 of my constituents in the York Valley condominiums in particular have voiced concerns. I want to put it on the record that they have very legitimate concerns. I will be continuing to work with the minister, the parliamentary secretary, and the government to ensure that their concerns are met and that the government continues to make sure that they are treated equally with other homeowners. Regardless of what happens with this bill, condominium owners will not have to fear discriminatory treatment and I will continue to work on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, the member talks about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its functions as a national entity.
I just want to point out that one of the main problems we have seen with respect to this government's direction over the last few years has been the consistent cutbacks to the CBC budget.
I point out that in 1984-85, the operations budget was some $943 million. In 1989-90, that has been cut to $812 million. In terms of the total budget, about $140 million will be cut over four years starting in 1990-91.
I want to point out that the CRTC said in its most recent licence renewal that the CBC could not fulfil its mandate at current funding levels. Since then we have seen further declines in the expenditures.
I would like to quote a comment from the CBC vice-president, Mr. MacEwen, who said: "You're right. We are getting squeezed each year. We have to factor in how we are going to do that. This year, which is 1989-90, they lost a 1 per cent real cut across the radio system. They managed to sustain their activity for one more year, but if we keep going, something is going to have to give."
As I mentioned to you earlier tonight, we heard announcements of major lay-offs in the CBC. I have the Library of Parliament at this time trying to find the details of just what are the extent of those lay-offs, but we understand they were announced tonight.
I would like to ask the member how he can justify the government's supposed commitment to a national broadcasting system in this country, a system that is responsible for defining our national unity and our national identity as a symbol of Canadianism. How can we continue to do this when in fact these substantial cuts in budget allocations to the CBC are being now realized in major job lay-offs? They are already short in terms of their ability to fulfil their mandate. How do you suppose they can continue to do it when they have to lay off even more workers?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate the member's question. Regardless of my own personal views on the matter, and regardless of the member's personal views on the matter, he and I both recognize that there is a difference of opinion with respect to the budgetary matters relating to the CBC.


That was pointed out very vividly on November 27 in a column written in the Ottawa Citizen by Marjorie Nichols in which she said that this fiscal year the CBC's budget is $1.4 billion of which $1 billion is a direct grant from the federal treasury. To put the CBC into perspective, it costs Canadian taxpayers as much as the RCMP, which received $1.2 billion this year. Actually the federal police generates more revenue, $526 million, than does the CBC, $439 million. The 10,500 CBC jobs theoretically cost the taxpayers of Canada about $100,000 each. If the CBC were sold, many of those jobs would be transferred to the private sector. If the CBC were privatized, absolutely everybody would be better off.
Marjorie Nichols goes on to say: "Given the new broadcasting act that provides the federal cabinet with expanded powers over broadcasting, the need for action is urgent. For the sake of Canadian democracy, the CBC ought to be put on the auction block."
I do not think everybody agrees with Marjorie Nichols, but that is the view of some Canadians. There is a difference of opinion with respect to this matter, and I think that is what democracy is all about. We are here to debate the various points of view. Marjorie Nichols' opinion is one thing, and the hon. member's opinion is another.

Mr. Speaker, I was in the prior Parliament with the hon. minister. I can recall with a great deal of precision many of his interventions which were very enlightened and very well formulated.

CF Cable has been asked many times to come in because the MATV system is working outside of the law. speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but this is a matter of opinion, not a point of order. I will therefore have to revert to debate.
Resuming debate. The hon. member for Winnipeg North.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on third reading of Bill C-40, an act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunications.
Before I proceed, allow me to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Mount Royal, for her leadership on this issue on behalf of our Liberal caucus.
This bill, in essence, should shape what we see on the television landscape in the future. It should make sure television will promote a sense of Canadian unity, a sense of our character as a people, of a people proud of our different origins and of a people with common shared values. But the bill is not clear in its vision and the government lacks the courage to commit funds to achieve the goal of promoting the Canadian nation on television.
This bill would have the power to change what Canadians see on their television sets. This is very important since broadcasting impacts on the way most people get their news, their entertainment, and then-understanding of our multicultural diversity. The medium of television should support a sense of shared values and a sense of national being. But there can be no genuine national being if we do not insist that the CBC is, at all times, to foster national unity. A renewal of this national mission as a mandate of CBC is vital to the continued survival of our nation.
Reaffirming national unity as a mandate is most relevant today, particularly when we witness segments of our country feeling alienated from each other and from a common whole. Our geography, our different languages and cultures and our common economic problems require a link if we are to continue to survive as a people and as a nation. Broadcasting serves as this essential linkage to bring together our aboriginal peoples, our founding settlers and our new citizens, adults and children, as Canadians.


Hence, I am pleased to see the retention in the proposed Broadcasting Act of the principle enunciated in the original Broadcasting Act of 1968:
The Canadian Broadcasting system shall be effectively owned and
controlled by Canadians so as to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the
cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada.
Unfortunately, only about 5 per cent of the programs presented to Canadians today on English television are Canadian in content. That is what we see, that is what our children see.
Since most of our children spend a lot of time watching television and learning from it, I fear that our children do not see enough programs that reinforce to them what it really means to be a Canadian.
Hence, ownership and programming content are two of the fundamental issues which a new broadcasting bill must address if it is to prove effective in the future. This bill fails in these twin challenges.
We have already seen the arrival of satellite communication and other technologies. The boundaries between nations have blurred. Broadcasting has made our planet truly a global village.
At the same time, there is palpable concern that these new technologies are being built only by a privileged few. This is not inherently wrong, but a danger lurks nearby. What the world will see, read and hear in the coming century could be coming from the hands of a few through mergers and take-overs. For example, new on-demand television services will likely fall in the control of a few, and if not licensed and regulated for Canadian content, would unduly profile and promote American and not Canadian programs.
Today, we have a watchdog organization that is supposed to ensure that the television medium is not concentrated in the hands of a few who can ignore important Canadian programming. That watchdog is the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission, the CRTC. But the CRTC has long been acknowledged as being somewhat of a toothless watchdog. Although it has the mandate to punish broadcasters who do not adhere to Canadian content standards by revoking their broadcasting license, the commission has never been strict with broadcasters who break the rules.
Government Orders
Bill C-40, instead of strengthening the watchdog duty of the CRTC, weakens that punitive power by adopting the approach of performance incentives. That is, it will reward networks who broadcast a sufficient number of programs with the stipulated Canadian content quota by waiving the annual license fee, which can be as much as one-third of a million dollars based on advertising revenues of $10 million. It will punish those who do not fulfil their obligations by making them pay part or all of the license fee.
But let us be realistic. The CRTC was always reluctant to use its power before, what reason do we have to believe that it will change now? Worse, the government will now have more veto powers over the commission's decisions. Hence, the networks can lobby the government to overrule unwelcome CRTC decisions. Besides, we all know that one-third of a million dollars fee is not enough to scare potential delinquent networks into showing more Canadian programs. These networks are some of the top money-making corporations in North America today. "The big networks can well afford to pay a $300,000 slap on the wrist", said Matthew Fraser of the Montreal Gazette in his column recently.
I believe the underlying issue behind this debate is money. Under Bill C-40, the CBC must "contribute to shared national conscience and identity", and make space for more cultural programs as opposed to commercial shows. These are admirable objectives, but I do not think the government has given much thought to the price-tag of its goals.
During its past four years in power, the Conservative government has cut $140 million from the already suffering network. Tonight in debate, we heard from the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James, based on some advance information he has, that at least another $100 million will be cut by the CBC affecting at least 10 radio stations, Radio Canada International, and the parliamentary channels.
One way in which the CBC has coped with these heartless cuts has been from the income the corporation gets from airing commercial programs. Now the government is telling the CBC to produce more cultural programs and move away from commercial programming. It costs a lot more to create a program than to buy one. One doubts that in this time of economic recession the government is going to give the CBC more funding in its next budget. I only hope that this pessimism would prove to be wrong.


Government Orders
Verily, I do not think the government is taking the important role of the CBC seriously. Telling the network to do more with fewer financial resources is unacceptable.
In conclusion, the CRTC and the CBC have very important roles to play in promoting a Canadian soul. The CRTC must be a watchdog with teeth. It must be able to ensure Canadian content quotas are filled and that the power of the television medium does not rest in the hands of a privileged few. The CBC must be given ample funding to produce good Canadian programming as well.
Bill C-40 does not properly address these issues. It should be a bill which promotes our sense of Canadian unity. We need a Broadcasting Act to make a difference to our airwaves. There will continue to be a deficit of programs showing who Canadians really are unless the government gives more power to the CRTC and more money to the CBC.
Canadians need to be shown the vision and the leadership with which to attain that vision. This side of the House is ready to form the government and to lead Canadians to a united country and people, linked via a new Broadcasting Act, an act that will broadcast to the whole world the true Canadian soul-united, caring, compassionate, and just.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the member on his fine presentation. I think he had a lot of very salient points to make.
I was particularly interested in the comments he was making on the CBC and its mandated function to serve as an instrument of national unity. He referred to these consistent cutbacks, $140 million more dollars slated over the next few years, and now we hear earlier tonight of even greater cuts in the offing. He raised the question as to how the CBC can possibly fulfil its mandate when it is essentially being knee-capped economically by the government that is looking to emasculate the corporation in terms of the role that it has to fulfil.
I do not know whether or not the member was here earlier tonight when I was speaking, but we had learned of just recently announced lay-offs in the CBC.
They were announced tonight. We did not have many details at that point. A little bit more has filtered in. In my discussions with the Canadian Press I found that these cuts are going to result in the closure of 10 regional stations that will either close completely or will be reduced to storefront operations. These are regional stations, regional centres, which have fulfilled a very important function in getting the Canadian news out to the scattered regions of this country.
I would like to ask the member the question I have been trying to ask the government. They certainly will not answer me. Perhaps the hon. member from the Liberal Party would care to comment on how these cutbacks and resultant layoffs can possibly be helpful to a corporation that is struggling to fulfil the mandate it has been given when it already knows it is short of funds and now, obviously, short of manpower.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his comments and for his question. He has truly identified the hypocrisy of this government, on the one hand trying to tell us that it is promoting the broadcasting institution in our country, and on the other hand trying to amputate it by cutting the financial resources necessary to support such an undertaking.
I cannot help but fully agree with my colleague and his concerns and I hope that before we vote on this bill the government will make a commitment, renew itself, change its heart, restore funding to this institution so that truly we can promote Canadian unity in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to my friend's intervention in this debate and I thank him and congratulate him for it. It was very thoughtful and well presented. I hesitated even to make an intervention, but I do it in a spirit of collegiality. I think I may have misunderstood the hon. member.
What I understood him to say is that, in the context of the financial crunch in which the CBC finds itself with declining commercial revenues, the government was telling the CBC to program more cultural offerings.


Perhaps I have missed something, but I am not aware that the government has ever told the CBC what to program.
I wonder if the hon. member could answer that.

Mr. Speaker, what I meant when I said that the CBC must be mandated to have Canadian content in its programming is that with this kind of mandate it has to create new programs of Canadian content. As yet we have very little of that in Canada. That type of undertaking will need support from the Canadian government. That is what I meant, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to one side of broadcasting and later about the erosion of the CBC.
Broadcasting is a powerful, unifying medium. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, is there anyone in this government who believes in the unity of this country? If so, why do they not stand up and defend federalism? Canada is falling apart, and nobody on the government side seems to care.
Mr. Speaker, withdrawing from the CBC's mission its mandate to promote national unity and to provide a forum for expressing our Canadian identity is only the tip of the iceberg.

Recently the Prime Minister highlighted the importance of national unity by saying: "Everything that we have accomplished as a country can be traced back to our sense of national purpose, to our national unity". If he really believes this, why did he remove the CBC's national unity goal? That is a quote from the hon. member for Mount Royal, who has led our party through this bill.
Why have we not heard of the Prime Minister going to his province and fighting for his country? He is willing to send Canadians to fight for Kuwait but he is too scared to venture into his own riding to fight for its place in Canada. The same goes for other ministers from Quebec. I find it completely reprehensible that ministers of the Crown have a half-hearted defence for the country they are sworn to defend and represent. I am tired of Conservative double-talk that tries to pander to both Canadian unity and Quebec independence.
Government Orders
The Conservatives and the New Democrats seem to be in the same boat on this issue. Their leaders cannot rely on their members from Quebec to stand up for their province's role in confederation. Mr. Speaker, I and my leader, the Hon. Jean Chretien, stand for a strong Canada with Quebec as a strong and prosperous partner in confederation. It would be a symbol of good faith to all Canadians, which includes the citizens of Saint-Laurent-Cartierville, to reinstate the CBC's role of promoting national unity.
It is the legitimate interest of a national body, such as the CBC, to make sure that our country is united and strong. It is for this reason that, without this mandate, I cannot support this bill at third reading.

Mr. Speaker, is that the way this government expects to create some harmony? Is it because the country is in such a mess that the government insists on removing from the CBC mandate the development of national unity and the broadcasting of some sense of Canadian identity? Is it because this government no longer believes in Canada, that it is gradually removing the development of national unity from the mandate? Naturally, the Minister will deny that it is his objective, but the facts tend to show that the reverse is true.

At a time when Canadians are divided over issues such as free trade, the GST, and the Constitution of the country, the country's national public broadcaster should be the purveyor of national unity. If we are to have a national personality, we have to weave all regions into a unified force. It is not by cutting funds that this government is helping Canada stay together. But, could that be its hidden agenda, letting Canada split apart and saying, "we did our best", knowing full well that they did not?
It is indeed sad to see that while this country is on the brink of disintegration, its national leadership has shirked its responsibility of fighting for a strong and unified Canada. Instead of the Prime Minister going on the road to hear how this country feels, instead of him going into Quebec and fighting for this country, he has reneged on his responsibility. It seems that the Minister of Communications has shirked his responsibility as well. He has withdrawn from the fight for Canada. He is obliged, by his duty to this country, to fight for Canada's unity. It is for this reason that he must reintroduce the national unity objective of the CBC.

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, how can the government ask the Canadian people to weave a stronger seamless web of national unity, when it does everything it can to tear it? Canadians are already offered very little cultural programming, especially outside Quebec. Does the government think that by cutting funds to the CBC and removing the development of national unity from its mandate, it will be able to offer better cultural programming to the French-speaking population of this country, and in particular better local cultural programming? Is the government genuinely interested in it or is it only a fagade?
Why now, Mr. Speaker? The unity of the country is holding only by a thread and it is now that this government wants to remove from the CBC's mandate the promotion of national unity and the expression of the forum to express Canadian identity. What is going on? What is this government afraid of? To take a stand?
Mr. Speaker, Quebec is already very seriously questioning its place within this country. If the state broadcaster is withdrawing from its promotion of national unity because this mandate is taken away from it, does that imply that this government has also decided to let Quebec go adrift? Is this the beginning of the quiet changes to allow for the possible break-up of this country?

It may seem like a small issue but it is with negative small issues that we break up a country. Liberals do not want this, nor do the Canadian people. You know who will be the person who is remembered for the dismantling of this country, this Prime Minister.
We need someone who will be committed to Canada. That is the Liberal Party and Jean Chretien. We can offer this vision to all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, we heard a lot from the members of the Bloc Quebecois. They told us that promotion of national unity is Canadian propaganda. I am sure the majority of Quebecers disagree with them. More than ever, Mr. Speaker, we have to create ties across Canada if we really care about this country. This move to take away the mandate for the development of national unity is a step in the wrong direction. We, in the Liberal Party, want to put the government back in the right direction. That is why we are absolutely against Bill C-40.

I would just like to touch on the gradual erosion of the CBC. The parliamentary secretary talked earlier about tax and sort of glossed over that there were not any, and that the CBC was servicing regional needs.
I quote the hon. member for Mount Royal again: "In 1985, this Conservative government began by cutting $85 million. In 1986-87, $5.6 million; 1987-88, $21.1 million;
1988-89, it came to 5.6 million; 1989-90, $5.8 million; and for the year 1991, $25.9 million".
When the hon. member for Mount Royal asked the minister to assure that there would be no further cuts to the CBC, he refused to say no. His only remarks to her were "It is with great pleasure that I note the member's suggestion".
One other point that the parliamentary secretary raised was the decision about national unity. I am not quite sure of his exact words, but he talked about the division of the board with a francophone committee and an anglophone committee. He said that this was approved by the chairman of the board. I wonder if he was talking about the chairman of the board of the CBC, Patrick Watson. I understand that when he appeared before the legislative committee, he expressed grave concern about dividing the CBC along linguistic lines. He is the chairman designate, and speaking with unequivocal and unanimous support of the CBC board of directors, he said: "Let me say that the board unanimously felt that this was both divisive in terms of the obligation of the corporation to be one".
I would be interested in hearing what the parliamentary secretary means when he says that we are not dividing the board of the CBC and that there were no parliamentary cuts planned. I hope the parliamentary secretary is right but we have yet to hear him say there will be no cuts. Could you please elucidate on this point?

Mr. Speaker, we have been speaking back and forth all night about the impact of the government's legislation and the impact of the government's continued expenditure cuts on CBC.
As we have been talking, the news has been filtering in and it has just become dramatically clear to us, startlingly clear to us, that the cuts that we are seeing take place tonight, that have just been announced, are the most severe cuts to take place in the history of the CBC.
It is estimated that the cuts are going to axe 1,200 people. They are going to eliminate local programs and are going to result in the closure of some 10 regional centres. This is just coming through the news now. The big loss will apparently be in local services. We already lost some 472 jobs earlier in the year. If the cuts go through, by next April a total of 1,600 jobs in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will have been axed.
The stations that will be axed, according to reports, are the regional stations in Calgary, in Saskatoon, in Windsor, Radio-Canada in Toronto, Quebec operations, the Goose Bay operation and operations in Newfoundland. It is a response to this government's $140 million cutting of the budget for CBC that is forcing the CBC board to have to take these kinds of drastic measures in order to make ends meet.
The argument that we placed earlier and the argument that is made ever more clearer tonight, is that this government is emasculating the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is essentially kneecapping it economically so that it can no longer fulfil its function. I wonder if my colleague who has just been speaking may wish to question the government as to how the CBC can continue to fulfil its mandate when this is the scenario that is facing the corporation right now.

Mr. Speaker, since I did not hear the news that were just announced-I hope that it is not the CBC-I am astonished. If the parliamentary secretary could explain another time what he meant when he said that there would be no cuts, because five minutes later, we heard that 1,200 jobs were cut and that 10 television stations would close. What does that mean? Could it be possible that he unintentionally mislead the House? Or

is he trying to make Canadians believe that the government is not really interested in national unity?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member asked a question and I will, by way of question and comment, endeavour to respond to it. I did make it clear earlier this evening that whatever announcements CBC will make tonight or tomorrow-I do not believe any announcement has been made.
It was on the news.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Lots of things are on the news. That does not mean that they have been announced or that they are factual. Indeed, if hon. members have the patience to wait for the announcement that it is believed will be made by the president of the CBC tomorrow, they may find that the government is assisting the CBC in its current difficulties.
Therefore I think it would be very inappropriate to cry havoc and raise alarms to the extent that it is implied that the government is butchering the CBC. The government is doing nothing of the sort. The government is endeavouring, in a time of difficult financial restraint, to nurture the CBC as best it can.

Mr. Speaker, the cuts referred to by the parliamentary secretary are absolutely outrageous. It is an outrage in Canada for the CBC to be announcing tomorrow the closure of two operations in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. Just imagine, a total closure of one station and a partial closure of another station. Of 10 cuts in Canada, two are in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador.

Government Orders
Could the parliamentary secretary or the minister, if he intends to come along to the House, explain why the Government of Canada is allowing the CBC totally to destroy its service to a great portion of Newfoundland and Labrador?
We have taken more cuts than any other province in Canada. It is an absolute outrage. Somebody from the government side should make an announcement tonight that it is going to object to those cuts and it is going to cancel them.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker, because since it is our 20 minute period, I do not want to give the minister the opportunity to take the floor again.

He is the parliamentary secretary, I apologize.
We say that Tory times are tough times. When I listened to the parliamentary secretary talking earlier about no budget cuts, he was saying: "Don't worry, be happy". speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: We are giving; we are not cutting.
I accept that.

Mr. Speaker, I realize the debate is getting rather circular, but many comments have been made reflecting the recently announced cuts which the media brought forward tonight.
The parliamentary secretary has essentially said that the government has had no part in these cuts. This is an argument that has gone back and forth between the two sides of the House tonight.
I wanted to make clear to the House and to the people of Canada that it was indicated in the newscast that these cuts were the response of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in terms of a necessary plan of action to follow through with the $140 million reduction in government spending the corporation must incur in the next four years.
