Point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will recognize the hon. member for Saint-Laurent-Cartierville for 30 seconds.
Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to put on the record again that the parliamentary secretary just told us that this government is not cutting but indeed is giving. Thank you again.

Mr. Speaker, we are debating Bill C-40 and the essence and the soul of this country as seen through communications.
Just before my hon. colleague from Saint-Laurent- Cartierville finished speaking, we had announcements on national television. We had what I would consider to be a near disaster in terms of communications, in terms of the means by which we not only bring the country together, and in terms of how we give an indication to all Canadians nation-wide what we are about. We are also talking about letting go 1,200 men and women with great expertise and experience in the communications field, in the electronics field, and in all other fields central and integral to the development of a high-tech, ultra-modem communications system, art system, and dramatic art system which identify and express for Canadians that element of Canadianism. All those people will be let go. The parliamentary secretary said that the government- and I think I am quoting him correctly; the "blues" will bear me out-is aiding, not cutting funds to the CBC.
It is almost outrageous that we should hear those kinds of statements. His colleague, the former parliamentary secretary for communications, earlier in the evening said: "I regret that there will be cuts"-and again I am sure that the "blues" will bear me out-"but when they come it is because they have to come".


Two hours later they came. They came with a slash. They came with a bang. Some 1,200 people, in addition to the 476 who have already been let go, will be let go by April 1, 1991 in order to make up a shortfall of $100 million, thanks to this government's lack of commitment, desire to kill the CBC, and any national means of communication, any national means of news, any national means of bringing Canadians together on a cultural point, on a news point, or on an information sharing point that was already there. The mechanism was there, and the government has decided that it is no longer worth maintaining.
We are seeing that through this Bill C-40. It is ironic that these announcements would have come on the eve of third reading of Bill C-40, which has been designed through this institution to bring awareness to all Canadians of the value of all institutions and instruments which make up our soul and our character. To have this kind of announcement tonight of all nights tells us that in essence what is being debated this evening is all for nought.
Parliamentarians will be unable to bring to the attention of all Canadians or convince them of the significance of this debate by bringing forth all important elements for consideration. In fact one of the lambs that will be sacrificed in these cuts will be the parliamentary channel, the vehicle for bringing our debates into the homes of each and every Canadian.
In addition, we can see from some of the cuts that the government is giving up on its sense of what Canada must be. I refer with great regret to one of the stations that will be cut. As a result of this government's action, one service that will no longer be available is Radio-Canada emanating in French from my own city of Toronto. There is nothing worse that one can say about establishing the whole concept of bilingual Canada, a Canada that is enriched by the differences that make up its whole, than to say that Radio-Canada will no longer be able to function out of the city of Toronto. It is a shame that this government would be associated with that kind of decision. It is an absolute criminal shame that the CBC would be put in a position where it has to make that kind of cut, because in addition to having to make up the shortfall of government finances toward the operation of this national institution, we learn through this report just
Government Orders
a mere one-half hour ago that we have to make up for a shortage of advertising revenues.
Advertising revenues that this government was mandating will no longer be allowed to go to the CBC because, of course, what we have to do is encourage the private local entrepreneur, the local broadcasters, who have been asking for that rich advertising dollar. I think it runs in the vicinity of $200 million in the province of Quebec alone and is at least equal to that throughout the rest of the country.
With the cuts we have seen this evening, we take a look at where we are going with Bill C-40. We can see that we are no longer engaged in an academic discussion. We are no longer talking about the esoteric merits of a communications system that may or may not satisfy the arts community, that may or may not satisfy those people who are in the broadcasting industry as journalists, as reporters and other announcers. No, we are talking about Canadians, each and every one of us, and when the government decides that it must take a cold, hard look which it suggests is the method with which it approaches everything because it is a good financial manager and, as a good financial manager, what it will do to make sure the bottom line is black. As always, what will happen is it will tear this country apart.
It was not that long ago that nations throughout the world decided that what they needed to do in the interests of establishing a national character is they would have to devote the energies and the resources of their nations toward the education of their people, to give them the sense of what each other was like. They did that through an education system.
They did it as well through a military system in order to bring people from various regions together through military service. They exchanged ideas, let everybody understand what the other was like. This gave them a sense of closeness through the regions, a sense of familiarity about culture. It broke down the barriers that come with linguistic differences, and encouraged and nourished and, in fact, cultivated all of those expressions of individual aspirations, community aspirations, regional and cultural aspirations that come through the expression of literature, prose, drama and theatre, all of those things which we would have hoped would have firmly imprinted themselves on the character of this country that we have all come to love.

Government Orders
We have all come to love this country, because for someone like me who had to come to this country thanks to the good decisions of his parents, but who now has his own children rooted deeply into the country and who now must decide on their own as to the Canadian character. Thanks to this government we no longer will have a vehicle to serve the interests that once were identified through an education system that would have imprinted a character.
Now, through this high-tech age, we see it is the communications system, a national system like the CBC that would have given us the opportunity, not only through the news, but through the arts, dramatic arts, prose and even through dubbing some of the productions emanating from the various regions, such as those from Quebec, southern Ontario and western Canada, and to be able to allow us to see each other as we are and as we would want others to see us and provide us with an opportunity to be sensitive to the issues of the day in Canada.
They are not only constitutional issues, they are economic issues, they are environmental issues. They are the issues that will determine how we will live in this country tomorrow and how we will see each other in the next century through that medium that could produce the appropriate documentaries, programs and bring together the experts who have the interests of this country at heart, to bring them together and to allow our children to allow us to be able to become informed and make the decisions that are environmentally appropriate, economically sound and culturally homogeneous for all of us, homogeneous in the sense of people who in their differences could still remain united. Mr. Speaker, the kind of cuts we have seen this evening bear out what Bill C-40 was intending to do, essentially balkanize and allow the regionalization of Canada by doing the same thing to the one system that held Canada together.
I do not need to remind my hon. colleagues on this side of the House. They have been most vigilant throughout this debate. I say that without appearing fawning, but most members in the House, not just from my caucus, have developed a great respect and admiration for our critic who has been absolutely terrific in bringing out all of those discussions, the technical components of this bill, and who has as well pointed out the philosophical repercussions of each and every one of the motions, of all of the changes, that are being applied through this bill.
Mr. Speaker, we are going to lose the opportunity, thanks to Bill C-40 and the government's action, negative, or inaction, which is at least dilatory, on issues that show the world what we as Canadians are. We have had some indication that perhaps, for example, Radio-Canada International might survive. We do not know for how long, but certainly it is a half-hearted commitment. It is no longer in the country's interest as far as the government is concerned.
Yes, there is the all-news service, but with the cuts we are going to find we will be unable to keep up with the demands and the rigours required in order to make sure that all Canadians receive the news on time, all the time, and in the fashion that would do professionalism honour, and in a fashion that would give an indication that the cultural differences, linguistic differences, regional differences, are put in the light which gives them the most favourable impression to all Canadians.
That is what has been missing in this country over the course of the last year and a half. We have not been given the opportunity to have the kinds of favourable impression we ought to have about each other, about each and every one of us, all of us, neighbours, friends and brothers and sisters in this country.
The government has not wanted to provide the appropriate legislative guarantees for such a mechanism. As I said earlier, it is interested more in ensuring that the regional approach to communication and through the ways we regulate, observe, and monitor that communication system, the CRTC, take place.
My colleagues have already pointed out how we have regionalized and balkanized the operations of the CRTC and we have essentially said we do not need nor do we want a national dimension to the kinds of decisions they will bring to bear on the broadcasting and communications system. I do not know how many ways that a parliamentary secretary, minister, or members of the government side can try to hide that fact, but the fact of


the matter is that when we no longer require a full executive of the CRTC to engage in decisions that relate to the communications system of this country, then we are essentially washing our hands of any kind of commitment that we ought to have to the national character of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I know you will be at one with me in this, a national character that allows for differences. It nurtures those differences and it recognizes that those differences actually provide energy and vigour to the character of Canada.
Bill C-40 for me, prior to hearing the cuts of this evening, already had meant that essentially the government, in addition to washing its hands of the duty, the obligation, the mandate to engage in establishing the national dimensions of this country was essentially opening the doors to what is already an insidious and all too pervasive effect on Canadian communication. That is the Americanization of both our culture, our language, our habits, and our views and perspectives on how the world should unfold, let alone how we as Canadians should develop our own potential. Colleagues on this side of the House have pointed out the vast majority of programming entering into this country viewed by our children. Maybe our children do not know enough yet, but at least we are in a position to make a choice. In making that choice we are offered few options; we have the American view of North America and we have the North American view of the world.
Thanks to Bill C-40, we no longer have the one unifying means, the financial resources and the mandate required to ensure that those resources bear themselves out in the kinds of programs that will give us a truly Canadian perspective, no matter from what region that Canadian perspective comes, a Canadian perspective nonetheless.
It has been of great sorrow to me to hear that the government, with Bill C-40, no longer feels that it is necessary to have any cautions in legislation to the infusion of more and more American broadcasting services, and yet there was a unanimous recommendation of the Communications and Cultural Committee of a mere three years ago that additional foreign networks not be allowed unless, of course, their programming was complementary to that of licensed Canadian services already.
Government Orders
No. It seems that the government is unwilling to strengthen the one instrument that would be there to enhance the Canadian character and in reneging on that opportunity it is essentially, deliberately weakening the possibility of a Canadian character.
We see that it is almost a logical consequence that the government would remove from Bill C-40 the national unity clause that was part of the CBC mandate.
I might remind the members, colleagues and one and all, those who feel especially strong about the CBC, about its potential. I do not want to get involved in the discussions of the mechanisms and the details one by one of the CBC programming and the hierarchy and the structure of the organization. I refer to the concept, to the potential that exists with that means of communication. That mandate that we are dropping from C-40 essentially told the CBC that it had to contribute to the development of national unity and to provide for a continuing expression of the Canadian identity.
By removing that clause, by no longer keeping us there, we are losing an opportunity to identify that Canada that is emerging. We are refusing to recognize the merits of those nations that have been part and parcel to the Canadian character as it has emerged through its first century of creation and, in fact, we are going to lose that umbrella organization that could reach out to all the emergence of a new Canada that is there, that is going to take its rightful place in the 21st century. Despite what this government would like to think, it is not the Canadian way to be immersed solely and simply in a parochial atmosphere of a North American environment with a very aggressive and very large neighbour. We have a country that is emerging because of the kinds of demographics that are allowing us to develop.
We have an opportunity to identify this new Canada. I cite, for example, just my own city of Toronto new Canadians see all of their news through three channels-Chinese, Portuguese and Italian. In combination, those three, on one local television area, represent more viewers than there are for the highest viewership of English language news. The CBC has an opportunity to focus in on that emerging type of Canada, to bring that and integrate it in with the already established mainstream cultures of Canada and, thereby, impress more of a new Canadian character on it. It can integrate the four

Government Orders
together, all the other new elements that come and without danger to each and any one of them, to give us an opportunity, through a vehicle such as the CBC, to learn more about each other, to identify each other, to familiarize each other with ourselves and to recognize all those common aspirations which we call Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence who, in a passionate way, covered a lot of bases.
First, I would like to ask him: Who said Radio-Canada would not operate out of Toronto? Those were the words he used, that Radio-Canada would not operate out of Toronto. I think he will find, since our only currency in this place is credibility, that that statement is not credible and perhaps he should check again.
Again, I would caution that it is pretty exciting, when we have a broadcasting debate going on and there is a big broadcasting story out there, to bring it in here. That is part of the game. We do those things. But I think we ought to be careful about the rumours or the stories that we present as facts in this place, because maybe this channel is being watched too tonight. We should, I think, give the CBC a break in terms of giving it some credit for its capability in managing its affairs which is, what I think, it is in the process of doing at this particular time.
The CBC is not the only instrument for Canadianiza-tion. It is the prime instrument, but not the only instrument.
I listened with some wry amusement to my friend when he was talking about the necessity to dub shows. I am sure he really did not intend it this way, but he was talking about dubbing shows from Quebec so that they could be understood and appreciated in English Canada. He went on to say that perhaps some from southern Ontario and even western Canada could be dubbed as well. He did not use those words, but the implication was there. I think I do not need dubbing to be understood by the hon. member.
The Americanization of the country, he felt, through the airwaves, would follow from the Balkanization that
would exist within the CRTC. That is, I believe, the string of logic that we were offered and challenged to follow. More and more Canadian programs are being viewed and many of those are produced by the private sector. Most of them are produced by the CBC, but many are produced by the private sector. I think we ought to give credit where credit is due.
I give just one example which was originated, with the help of Telefilm, by a broadcaster in my own community and that was Bye, Bye Blues, one of the finest Canadian films to have been produced in recent years.
Finally, I do want to comment on the hon. member's challenge, which I share, and that is that the Canadian broadcasting system, as a whole-and he singled out the CBC-ought to reflect the new Canada and its various components. Well, there may be some things that the framers of this legislation-and I include my friend, the hon. member for Mount Royal, as one of the framers of this legislation.
I'm feeling uncomfortable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
She is getting uncomfortable.
There is one thing that we succeeded in doing and of which we can all be proud and it is that the system-not just the CBC, but all components of the system-is mandated by this bill to reflect Canada in all its diverse glory, but at the same time to stimulate a national consciousness and identity.
I come now to the multicultural reality of our country and the multicultural mandate which is imposed on the system, for the first time, in this bill. I would say, Mr. Speaker, not only in that which is portrayed on the air, in radio and in television, but more particularly and most significantly-and my friend from Mount Royal fought with me on this, and Lynn McDonald fought with us at the outset, on the same side I should rush to say-that the operations clause of this bill mandates that stations in their operations will also reflect the reality of the new Canada. That means that there is no escape byway of the floor of 100 employees such as with the federal employment equity legislation. There is no such floor. Every broadcast operation-be it cable, radio, television, or whatever-must follow the appropriate methods to make sure that the operations of that station and what goes on the air reflect the reality of the new Canada.

Mr. Speaker, one is almost encouraged by the manner, if not the content, of the hon. parliamentary secretary because he has essentially been saying this is a very credible bill. He has pointed out-and I want to start from the last point, to do him credit-that there is an element to the bill that is encouraging, and has been received positively by all members of the House. That is that the CBC be required to reflect the new ethnocultural, multicultural, multi-racial character that is Canada.
In the private sector as well.

Yes, in the private sector as well, as my colleague for Mount Royal says. That is a positive step.
I know that the parliamentary secretary will recognize that by the turn of the century, close to 50 per cent of the population will no longer be associated with the initial two founding nations, in the constitutional sense, of the country. I know that there is much debate about that and that is why I say, in a constitutional sense. This is no aside to the groups of aboriginal Canadians who are very much a part of the Canadian character.
We have to move from that point which is acceptable and I thank the parliamentary secretary for having worked hard to ensure that that that be one of the items in Bill C-40.
On the others, I think we have to come back to a word that he used earlier on and that is the question of credibility. The government has its own vacuum of credibility when it comes to many of the issues that the parliamentary secretary is attempting to defend.
When I made reference to the newscast of about 20 minutes prior to my intervention, I have very good reason to believe that that national broadcast was based on information that all of us will share once again tomorrow morning. The retelling those facts as they were projected gives us an opportunity to enrich the debate. If some of those broadcast facts are not correct, then I think that the debate tomorrow will point that out, just as the debate today is pointing out all the vacuums and shortcomings of the government's position on this bill.
One of the things that is important for us to understand is that, if all of the consequences of Bill C-40 come to pass, as we have been given an indication that they are already coming to pass, we will not be favourably served by small private sector corporations that will fill in the
Government Orders
vacuums of CBC at a local level, if in fact they will have the potential for so doing. What will those people from Calgary, Comer Brook or Windsor do? They are accustomed to getting a first-class news service, a first-class exchange of the character of Canada. What will they do and to whom will they turn?
One can see that once we remove another Canadian channel, another component, a subsidiary of CBC, from our dial, the vacuum is quickly filled. It is a fact of life, because we live along the American border, that many of the American stations will receive much more attention than they normally would. We will suffer as a result because we will not have the same access to that which is essentially Canadian that we had a mere few hours ago.

[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Inuktitut.]
I am very pleased to speak on this Bill C-40, the new Broadcasting Act for Canada. I am pleased to participate in this debate, because it has taken the government several years to get to this point.
In 1985 the Ministry of Communications established a task force on broadcasting policy. Its report, also known as the Caplan-Sauvageau Report, was reviewed by the Standing Committee on Culture and Communications. That committee submitted four reports with numerous recommendations to the government for the drafting of the new legislation.
In the last Parliament in June of 1988, the government brought forward Bill C-136, but because a federal election was called Bill C-136 did not get through the Senate. Bill C-40, introduced in October 1989, is virtually identical to Bill C-136 which died on the Order Paper.
There is a general consensus that a new Broadcasting Act is needed. The current Broadcasting Act goes back to 1968. Communication technology has outpaced the 1968 act in many ways and in many respects. There is a need to take into account technological developments since 1968 and the present global realities.
This bill, however, is not perfect. It has flaws and deficiencies which my colleague, the hon. member for Mount Royal, has tried to correct by proposing amendments both in the legislative committee which studied this bill and at report stage over the past several weeks.


Government Orders
My colleague from Mount Royal, my party's spokesperson on the communications issue, has spoken ably and eloquently about the concerns we have about Bill C-40. I will touch on some of them briefly.
We are concerned about the possible constitutional challenges to this bill. We are concerned about the government's decision to drop the CBC's mandate to contribute to the development of national unity and to provide for a continuing expression of national identity. The government instead wants the CBC to contribute to national consciousness. That is a cop-out. This government is copping out on Canada.
It is no wonder this country has gone through so much constitutional agony and turmoil under this government. This government does not want the country's national broadcasting agency to contribute to the national unity. Unity encompasses so much more than a simple consciousness. We can be conscious of a lot without being unified.
We regret as well that this bill will not make Radio Canada International, the parliamentary television network, or the CBC northern service part of its mandate. Both the Caplan-Sauvageau report and the Standing Committee on Culture and Communications have recommended that these services be incorporated into new broadcasting legislation. Each of these services is a vital component of our Canadian broadcasting system and incorporating them specifically in this bill would have given them official recognition and a parliamentary confirmation of continuity.
I would like to take a moment to elaborate on the CBC northern service. This service is absolutely vital to the northern communities, some of which have no other available broadcast service. We do not want to see any reduction in the northern service. CBC's northern service covers the Yukon, N.W.T. and the James Bay and Nunavik regions of northern Quebec. The service spans four time zones and more than one-third of the total land mass of Canada.
There are 100,000 northerners living in the northern service region, most of them aboriginal peoples. Cree people constitute 90 per cent of the James Bay population. The Inuit are 85 per cent of the population in the Beaufort, Central, Keewatin and the Baffin regions of the Eastern Arctic, and also of northern Quebec.
In the rest of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, native people make up about 30 per cent of the population and are the majority in most of the smaller communities in the far north.
CBC northern service radio produces more than 200 hours of programs each week. Half of those hours are produced in seven aboriginal languages: Inuktitut, Slavey, Dogrib, Chipewyan, Inuvialuktun, Gwich'in and Cree.
CBC northern service television produces four weekly program series: Focus North, which is a weekly northern current affairs program; Denendeh K'eh, a multilingual Dene language program which combines life style features with topical current affairs; Aqsamiit, an Inuktitut language current affairs information program based in Iqaluit; and Maamuitaau, a Cree language program of features and issues produced by northern service in Montreal.
CBC northern service also assists six northern native broadcasting societies in distributing their programming. One is IBC, the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation for the Eastern Arctic, which just recently had a $600,000 cut to its budget and is now in danger of cutting more programming. It has already cut one regional office in Cambridge Bay in my riding. It is also in danger of cutting a veiy popular TV series which is produced in Baker Lake and is enjoyed by many, many children in the eastern Arctic because it is in the Inuktitut language.
We have also received support from various people from the north, including the regional director for the government of the Northwest Territories in the Keewatin region. He would like us to make sure that there are no cuts to any Inuktitut programming in the CBC northern service as well as other people from Iqaluit and elsewhere in the eastern Arctic.
These aboriginal communications societies are essential components of the Canadian broadcasting system because they do a lot to promote the cultural identity of the aboriginal people in the far north.
We appreciate the references made to the aboriginal people in the bill, but we fear this government is just paying lip service to aboriginal communications needs. We found two references to aboriginal people in Bill C-40. One reference says that the Canadian broadcasting system should reflect the special place of aboriginal peoples within Canadian society.

The second reference says that programming which reflects the aboriginal culture of Canada should be provided "as resources become available for the purpose". There are two points that I would like to make on this comment: Why has the government refused to include aboriginal languages in this bill? Why is programming reflecting aboriginal culture limited by available resources when throughout the last number of months the emphasis by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and by the Prime Minister of Canada has been that it is doing more for the aboriginal people than has ever been done. On the other hand the government is cutting aboriginal languages programming and also cutting the means of communicating among the aboriginal people.
I would like to comment that the National Aboriginal Communications Society's office had to close because of cutbacks.
Their Micmac News has been shut down. Those are some of the aboriginal means of communications which have been cut by this government.
This clause that I pointed out earlier means nothing in the light of massive cutbacks that the government made to the aboriginal communications in last April's budget.
I repeat: Budgets have been cut. Papers have folded. Offices have closed, and employees have lost their jobs.
The impact of the cuts have been devastating. Why did the government do this? We cannot believe this government is sincere about supporting aboriginal culture with this bill when it is directly responsible for the demise of several aboriginal media, since this bill was introduced in October 1989.
It is a sad but telling fact that the government restored almost all of the funding it cut to women's centres in last April's budget but would not do the same for the Aboriginal Communications Society.
Government Orders
I am glad that the women's centres got their funding back, but women voters outnumber aboriginal voters. The women had an ally in this instance in the Minister responsible for the Status of Women. She intervened.
Aboriginal people, unfortunately, had no such advocate. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, who should have intervened on our behalf, did nothing. In fact, he said that aboriginal communications had enough funding. Meanwhile, they are closing their offices, newspapers, and programming on radio and television were being cut.
It is because of situations like this that aboriginal people have no faith in the government's words. This government says one thing and does the opposite. This government professes support for the aboriginal people out of one side of its mouth, while on the other side it is cutting and slashing that support.
In conclusion, I can only be cynical about this bill. I am cynical about this government's commitment to aboriginal communications, to the CBC and the CBC's northern service.
We want to see the components of our national broadcasting system protected and enhanced. We want to preserve national unity within the CBC's mandate.
The CBC has for years been a bond which linked us from sea to sea to sea, and we share it like we share no other Canadian Constitution. The railway went east to west. CBC went east, west and north. Removing national unity from the CBC's mandate is a big mistake.
I urge the Government of Canada to rethink its position through this bill, and realize that it helps in a small way in keeping national unity by retaining the promotion of national unity as part of its mandate.
I stress that the national unity component has to be retained because this government does not understand how to promote national unity. Its concept of promoting national unity is by rolling the dice. I do not think that is a very good way of promoting national unity.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments that my colleague in the Liberal Party has made with regard to the implications of Bill C-40 respecting the native broadcasting programs.


Government Orders
It is this, in particular, that I wanted to go into depth a little more with. Since the Northern Native Access Program was established in 1983, it has been cut back substantially. I should point out that it was created at that time to ensure that northern native people have fair access to the distribution systems to help maintain their languages, cultures and that programming that was relevant to native concerns to ensure that these programs could be produced and provided in the northern communities. When it was originally created, it had a budget of almost $40.3 million over four years. In 1985 and 1986, this was reduced to less than $34 million and in subsequent years was reduced again and again. The
1989-90 funding was frozen at $13.2 million and now in this last hatchet job to the program, it has been cut back to $11.3 million. We have seen a drop from $40 million for the native northern broadcast access program to $11.3 million, an incredible decrease in expenditures for what should be a priority commitment of this government in terms of allowing the expression of a native identity in our north country.
According to the Nielsen task force when it made comment on the program, it stated with regard to the program: "It shows promise as an effective tool for meeting special native broadcast needs and should be continued".
I just want to quote comments made by the Waterways Native Communication Society when they were discussing with the communications committee on a previous bill, Bill C-126, but it reflects on this particular bill. They noted the importance of having a native communications system in the north. They said:, "It is the Waterways' view that there needs to be more aboriginal language productions, programs produced by aboriginal people for aboriginal audiences. Special emphasis must be given to the production of children's programming. The production of more aboriginal language programs should at least begin to counter balance the heavy influx of irrelevant southern programming".
That is a pretty significant statement. In reference to that statement, and also in reference to the drastic budgetary cuts that we have seen take place, I want to ask the member, because I think he has perhaps very particular knowledge of the impact of these budgetary cuts, just how specifically can he see the latest round of cuts and the over-all strategy of sort of economically strangling this northern native broadcasting system?
How does he see it impacting with this Bill C-40 legislation?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. One of the things that we have often heard in this House through my colleague from Western Arctic and myself as well is the danger of something like 38 aboriginal languages being forgotten because of the assimilation of the English and French languages. I would like to stress that there are a few languages that have a very good chance of surviving, of which Inuktitut, my language, is one. However, that too can be in danger of going if the aboriginal language programming by the CBC is cut any further.
As my hon. colleague pointed out, a cut of something like $28 million in a seven year period does not only reflect that it has gone down to $11.3 million. Over the years the cost of living, the cost of services, everything has gone up but the funding has gone down. As much as we appreciate the hard work that our regional directors in the north in the aboriginal communities have done to ensure aboriginal communications programming within the CBC within their ability to promote aboriginal languages, it is getting extremely difficult to keep going, especially among the communities which are a minority within their province or within their regions. We are very lucky in the eastern Arctic that we are a majority and, unless there are more drastic cuts in the CBC northern programming-which I would dearly hope not-we have a good chance of keeping on with our Inuktituk programming.
As I pointed out earlier, programs that are closely associated with the CBC northern service have been cut because of the government's willingness to cut, through the Secretary of State, the programs that were very popular among the children. I again would like to refer to that children's program and another program where there was a character called Johnny in the IBC program. It is in danger of being cut as well.
As I pointed out earlier, there has been offices closed. I, again, thank the hon. member for his question and I would like to stress how important it is that not only should the government not cut any more, it should raise the funding to more acceptable levels within the aboriginal communications societies and communications programs.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Malpeque.

I appreciate this opportunity to participate in this very important debate on Bill C-40, an act that removes the CBC's mandate to promote national unity and provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity.
Throughout my lifetime and, I am sure, for generations, dating back to Confederation, Canadians have often posed the questions: What is a Canadian? What is our identity? Are we any different from the British or the Americans? What is there to being a Canadian, and what is it that binds us together?
These are questions on which a thesis could be written and they are questions to which certainly I cannot do justice tonight in this short period of time, but I would like to share with this House some of my thoughts on Canadian identity and why it is essential that we continue to protect and promote it through vehicles such as CBC.
We are certainly unique from all other peoples and all other nations. For instance, there are few Canadians who would accept being considered one and the same with Americans. Now this should not be mistaken as anti-American. It is simply that Canadians consider themselves somehow distinct from our neighbours to the south.
Canadians have a reputation for being a tolerant people, exacting, even welcoming diversity, a people who love the land and the outdoors, a nation that promotes individual freedom yet respects the rule of law.
Some people have said that Canada lacks a common culture or identity because we are too diverse. I disagree with that statement. In fact, I believe that diversity has traditionally been a major component of our identity, while tolerance is our Canadian way of life.
We have heard an analogy of the quilt made of rags. Alone, a rag does not produce warmth or protection from the elements. When each rag is sewn together by a common thread to make up a quilt, what was once a pile of rags is now a quilt capable of keeping a child warm and secure on a cold winter's night. Like that quilt, our country is made up of many diverse cultures. When these cultures are woven together by a common thread, they make up one of the most beautiful countries of the world. However, if one removes that common thread,
Government Orders
the quilt will fall apart. If we remove the common threads that hold us together as Canadians, we may well cause our country to fall apart.
CBC is a common thread that links Canadians together across our land. Because of our geography, there are few means at our disposal to link the dairy farmer in Prince Edward Island with the plight of Pacific coast fishermen, the lumberjack in British Columbia to the fishermen in my riding in Malpeque, or the anglophone Albertan oil rig worker with the francophone shopkeeper in Quebec, northern Ontario or New Brunswick.
If it were not for the CBC in my riding of Malpeque, Prince Edward Island, Islanders would be less likely to identify with the concerns and problems of other Canadians. In fact, we would be less likely even to be aware of those problems.
As The National news on CBC unites Canadians from coast to coast, in my province of Prince Edward Island the supper hour show Compass links Islanders from North Cape to East Point, the farmer from Clyde River to the business person in Charlottetown, the fisherman in Rustico to the tourist operator in Brudenell. What I am really saying here is that it creates a better understanding, a sense of community, where disparity seems to be the order of the day.
The province of Prince Edward Island is completely surrounded by water. Besides the ferry and the airplane, perhaps our most important link to the rest of Canada is the media and the CBC. The CBC provides Islanders with a national and provincial perspective on the issues of the day.
The federal presence in our province has already been diminished by the policies of this government. The Tories have already taken away CFB Summerside. They have closed some of our rural post offices. They have abandoned the CN freight rail services. They have cancelled our direct flight to the nation's capital from Prince Edward Island through Air Canada. They have cut our ferry subsidies which link us to the rest of the country. They have cut transfer payments to the province, reducing the federal commitment to our schools, hospitals, and social services. Now they want to remove from the CBC its mandate to promote national unity, which in this time of intense parochial and regional disparity may have the effect of further isolating Islanders from the rest of the country.


Government Orders
This government which has jeopardized the future of our country through its leader's roll the dice approach to national unity now wants to further put at risk our ability to come together as Canadians. The approach that this government has taken with this legislation is indicative of the government's over-all approach to national unity and its abdication of responsibility and leadership. Removing the promotion of national unity from CBC's mandate is not required, is not desired, and its timing could not be worse.
I am proud tonight to say that the Liberal Party is opposed to removing CBC's mandate to promote national unity. I thank you for the opportunity to stand in my place tonight to state my views on the ramifications that Bill C-40 may have for the people of Prince Edward Island and for all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak on third reading of this bill respecting broadcasting and to express my concern about this bill, as I did very briefly last evening at report stage.
In my view this is a most ill-conceived measure. We recognize in our party that the bill contains some good points. We needed a new Broadcasting Act in Canada, and this bill provides some assistance in that regard. However, there are serious shortcomings in the bill that we as an opposition, and particularly the hon. member for Mount Royal, has sought to correct by moving numerous amendments to this bill.
Today we witnessed the spectacle of the government voting down every one of those amendments. None was agreed to today; they were all voted down. Only amendments to this bill proposed by the government were accepted. I think I am correct in saying that, in every case. I find that a shocking contempt of Parliament, a shocking abuse of the rights of members to participate and discuss government measures and to try to correct them.
Certainly there is lots to correct in this bill. Even the parliamentary secretary, who I know missed that because he was very busy with other matters, would agree with me that this was a very high-handed approach on the part of his minister. Throughout the debate at the report stage, the minister refused to participate in the discussions, refused to propose the government's amendments by way of explanation to the House, and refused to comment on the very reasoned statements and speeches made by members on this side of the House. I think it showed a contempt of Parliament that we have not witnessed in this House for many years, and I am disappointed that the government took that approach.
Another indication of that contempt, I submit, is the requirement that we be sitting here at this hour of the night discussing this bill. The rules for parliamentary debate are pretty clear that the House normally adjourns at six o'clock. We were unable to obtain agreement from the government that a reasonable amount of time, that is more than one day, would be allowed for third reading debate on this bill. It was made clear that if we could not make such an arrangement time allocation would be used, and so we agreed to it.
As a measure to allow members on this side who wanted to express their concerns to participate in the debate, we had a motion passed yesterday. The government said: "We will agree to allow you to sit after six o'clock. You can debate this bill to your heart's content, but there will be terms".
What were the terms? Let us just look at the little motion passed in this House yesterday afternoon by unanimous consent. In part it read:
That on TUesday, December 4, 1990, the House continue to sit beyond the ordinary hour of daily adjournment, with quorum calls and dilatory motions not receivable during such period of continued sitting-
They wanted to get it out of the way.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
What does that mean? What does it mean that there will be no quorum calls or dilatory motions? What it means is that the government does not have to ensure that there are 20 members in this House to keep the House sitting. That is what it means. That is why there is almost no one here. It also means that government members can all go home and go to bed, because they are not interested in participating in the debate. There has only been a handful of them participating tonight. I congratulate the parliamentary secretary for his efforts in that regard. He is the last one here. I congratulate him for participating, and I am glad he did, but his colleagues might have and they chose not to do so.


The reason they chose not to do so was that they did not want to sit here and listen to the criticisms of this bill, which this opposition is entitled to bring forward and raise in this House. Members of the government have fled because they do not want to listen to those criticisms. I submit again that that displays an enormous contempt of this institution, an enormous Tbiy arrogance of the worst kind.
They do not want to listen to criticisms. They say: "What we have proposed is perfect or as close to it as we are going to get, and no one in Canada can tell us that this could be improved in a way that we have to listen to or that we will make any changes". That is exactly what has happened.
The hon. member for Mount Royal has tried to make changes and even members of the New Democratic Party have tried to make changes. We have proposed amendments to this bill, and the government does not even want to sit and listen to the discussion. The government says: "You people can talk until nine o'clock tomorrow morning, all night if you want, but we are not going to be here and listen to you. You cannot move a dilatory motion, so there are no naughty tricks you can play on us. There are no quorum calls, so our members go home and go to bed", as they have done, "nothing can happen that will upset the House. It will continue to sit and we will not lose our bill".
That, Mr. Speaker, is contempt of Parliament. It is a disgrace. It is unfortunate that the opposition, in order to get its day in court on this bill has to agree to those kinds of terms and conditions to keep the government happy, to allow us to have a fair and reasoned debate.
I want to turn to my concerns about the changes this bill proposes to the CBC, particularly to the division of the CBC into two parts, the English wing and the French wing. That is exactly what the government has proposed in this iniquitous legislation.
This government is the architect of disunity in Canada. Never ever, since the conscription crisis in 1917 has there been so much discord and disharmony in Canada as we have today. The sole reason for that discord and disharmony is the actions of the Prime Minister and his cabinet who are incompetent, who are divisive, who have no idea how to govern this country, and who, since June, have
Government Orders
been sitting here twiddling their thumbs, wondering, "What do we now?". They have no more sense of direction than the man in the moon.
The roll of the dice.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The roll of the dice signifies their policy. They divide the country. They pit region against region. They are tearing apart the federal government. They will give anything to the provinces. They will sell us all to the United States. They have done it all. They have done all of it in the name of trying to govern the country. They say they are a government. I say they are a disgrace. They should resign immediately because they are such a disgraceful government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Are you having trouble keeping a straight face?

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I have no trouble keeping a straight face on that one. The parliamentary secretary thinks this is a joke. This government is a disgrace.
As I say, the amazing thing was to listen to the Prime Minister in Question Period yesterday. I could quote him, Mr. Speaker, but I will not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Please do.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
He was trying to blame Jean Chretien, the leader of the Liberal Party for discord in Canada. Of all the outrageous claims! Everyone else is to blame except the Prime Minister. It was the Prime Minister who weakened this country. It was the Prime Minister who started dismantling the federal government.
Let us go through the list of organs of the state that have been dismantled under this government. VIA Rail, slashed and cut. It was one of the first national enterprises we ever had in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
1997, my foot. VIA Rail was established by Sir John A. Macdonald, the Father of Confederation. It was built as a term of Confederation. VIA Rail has been slashed and cut by this government in a way that it has never been slashed and cut before.
Petro-Canada is now being sold. We have the bill before this House. It will be back here shortly, if it is not now. Fire sale prices for selling off the national assets of Canada for which Canadians paid millions of dollars.

Government Orders
Air Canada. Canada's national airline that provided essential transportation services across this country-sold off. The Post Office. Rural closures right across the country-slash, slash, slash, cut out rural services for Canadians. It created two classes of Canadians, those who in live in urban municipalities with door-to-door delivery and those who deal with supermailboxes because they live in new subdivisions; and those in rural Canada who had their service slashed and cut. That is what this government is doing.
That's harmonization.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for Okanagan-Shu-swap says it is harmonization. It may be, but it creates a great deal of disharmony in the country. I am sure he would agree that that is so.
Then we have the free trade agreement where everything is sold to the United States. Give away our energy resources. Give everything away. I could go through that at length, Mr. Speaker, but I will not-
Even our water.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Even our water, as the hon. member for Mount Royal says, is being given away.
Then we have the Prime Minister giving away the CBC by slashing and cutting. We heard about the cuts tonight. Ten stations across the country about to be closed and the parliamentary secretary says that these are not cuts. He says the government is giving.
I am afraid that his trip abroad has deranged him. He must have got something mixed up because when we hear these rumours on the radio, on the CBC particularly, they invariably turn out to be true, it seems to me.
I have hardly ever heard a CBC news account of rumours and stories about government cuts and slashes that have not turned out to be true. Usually they are on the light side. Usually the cuts are worse than were proposed in the story. If we on this side have been wrong in talking about the cuts tonight, we will hear about it in the morning. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will stand up and apologize to the House tomorrow if, in fact, all these cuts and slashes that have been announced tonight happen. I look forward to hearing him eat his words if that is the case.
Finally, if that list of destruction of federal government programs is not enough, then we can turn to the Prime Minister's roll of the dice for Canadians last summer. Thlk about hypocrisy, talk about blaming the leader of the Liberal Party, who is not even a member of Parliament at the moment, for the problems that Canada faced last June.
The Prime Minister is the one who had the responsibility to lead this country, but he insisted on raising the stakes. Instead of saying yes, there may be a problem with the Meech Lake Accord we have negotiated, we may have to try and do something else, he said, it is sign or else. That was his message. That is what drove the wedge between the premiers. That is what so sowed disunity in Canadians hearts, because they said they are being forced into a take it or leave it proposition in respect of their Constitution and they did not like it. Canadians from coast to coast were up in arms about it and the Prime Minister kept denying it. He said everybody supports this.
There was serious disunity on the issue, but the facts never bothered our Prime Minister. He says, "I am not bothered by the facts, I don't care what Canadians think. All I care is that I got the votes from the premiers, they all signed, they have to then follow through and it is sign or else, it is sign or else!" He said it for weeks and weeks and weeks, right up until the last minute and then he did his roll of the dice and it did not work.
Now he is saying the reason it did not work is because of Jean Chretien. What did he do, weight the dice? What did he do, jump on the dice when they were in mid-air? Did he catch them and throw them another way? What utter rubbish! Yet the Prime Minister has the nerve to stand in this House, of all places, and make that kind of palpable nonsense of a statement.
The parliamentary secretary says it is quite true. I think he needs his head examined, because I do not think there is another reasonable person in this room who thinks that that is quite true and I ask him to find one. Find another person in this room who agrees that the Prime Minister's statement is true. The hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap does not think so. The hon. member for Mount Royal does not think so. I am sure that the Speaker, learned as he is, does not think so. So who does? No one else thinks so. The parliamentary secretary is outnumbered and outvoted on that one.


In my submission, the government is absolutely incapable of achieving or working toward national unity in Canada. This bill is just another example of its abject failure in that regard. What the government has done by this bill is say that it is not going to even try to pull Canada together. It is not going to even try to keep the national broadcasting system of Canada as a national institution. It is going to divide it in half along linguistic lines, just what Canada needs. Instead of trying to create a bilingual, bicultural country that operates as a national unit, it is going to divide the CBC so that one group can speak one language and listen to broadcasts in one language and the other can do the other. It will simply tailor the broadcasting systems to suit the audiences and forget the idea of a national audience of national appeal, of a national system, of a system that tries in some small measure to unite the two language groups so that we share the common culture, we share some common values, we share some of the advantages of having two languages and two cultures operating in a country. I am not meaning to exclude any others by that statement.
This government is incapable of that kind of vision. It is incapable of that kind of understanding of Canada, if you like, and it has been an understanding that has been ingrained in thousands of Canadians for all of my lifetime. I have no trouble with the concept. I think it is a great concept. I think it is a great country we live in, but this government seems hell bent on breaking it up. Their whole attitude is cut services, break the federal government down so that Canada's constituent parts can go and do their own thing, weaken the ties that bind us from east to west, weaken the national ties that help hold us together through things like the CBC and let every province just go off and do its own thing, do it with the United States so everything will be north and south, forget about the east-west tie, make all trade deals south of the border and do not worry about trading with the other provinces. We are not concerned about a lack of free trade between the provinces is this government's approach. Why should it care? Because it is quite prepared to have us do all our trade with the United States, that is why.
It is quite prepared to say: "Well, if Americans come in and buy up all of Canada that is too bad for Canadians. It is the best thing because it is the marketplace at work". That is its approach.
It is not the right approach. It is not the way Liberal governments have done it and they have been in power for most of this century and have done an extremely good job of governing Canada.
Government Orders
What we have had since 1984 is the destruction of the fabric of Canada that has been built up through generations of governments in the past. The hon. member who is here must know that the CBC was, after all, a creation of a Conservative government, one of the few on the list. Nevertheless, it is there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Unemployment insurance.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member says unemployment insurance. I do not think he is right in that. I think he will find that unemployment insurance was in fact done by a Liberal government. My recollection is that the amendment to the British North America Act as it was at the time which made unemployment insurance possible for the federal government was in fact passed at Westminster as a result of a request from this Parliament when it was under the control of the Liberal government. I believe it was in 1949.1 may be wrong in my date. It was certainly post-war and it certainly was not a Conservative government. The first one after the war in my recollection was in 1957, and we all know what a disaster that government was. It was the worst one we have had in Canada before this one.
Almost as bad as this one.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Almost as bad as this one. To look at it from the other perspective, as the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap has so ably put it. It is almost as bad as this one.
He doesn't agree.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. parliamentary secretary looks as though he does not agree. Probably the realization has just hit him as to how bad this government is. I am glad he has been sitting and paying such close attention to my speech so that message can sink in.
Mr. Speaker, I think my pleas in this case are falling on deaf ears. I would like to say "no ears" but the parliamentary secretary is here and I appreciate that. But I am afraid that even he will not be able to convince the minister that urgent changes are needed to this bill if it is going to be acceptable.

Government Orders
We can only hope that when the bill gets to the other place, if and when it passes on the vote tomorrow-and perhaps some of his colleagues will see the folly of their ways and vote with us to defeat it-we can hope there will be significant changes made by the other place and the bill will come back here and we can adopt those changes.
Sober second thought, Mr. Speaker, seems to work in some cases and possibly, although this bill has been before this House since what, March?
March 19.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
You would have thought that the government might have drawn a sober breath some time between March and now and realized that this bill needed change and might have adopted some of the amendments we proposed, but it has not worked.
Perhaps in the other place reason will prevail and we will see some significant changes to get rid of the more odious provisions in this bill, particularly the one that, in my submission, will lead to further division and discord in Canada by dividing the CBC effectively into two corporations. I submit that is not in the best interests of Canadian unity. It is not in the best interests of Canada. It is not in the best interests of the CBC, and it is definitely not in the best interests of a government which believes that Canada is worth saving as a single entity.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know quite where to begin but I am going to tiy to respond to some of the points my hon. friend from Kingston and the Islands has made.
It was his predecessor from that constituency who essentially was the architect of the bill that is now before us, and a wise and sage minister she was.
It is not proposed that the CBC be divided into two parts, and I think the hon. member knows it. The CBC is proposed to have two standing committees of its one board of directors, in each of which committee would participate the president and the chairman, in order to bridge the two solitudes in this country. That is the sole and only purpose of that particular proposal in the bill.
I did not say that cuts would not be happening to the CBC tomorrow. What I did say is that the government was not imposing any cuts on the CBC. In fact the government would be helping the CBC financially in the dilemma that it is now confronting.
On the question of national unity we heard again, Mr. Speaker, the line tonight that he or she who opposes the idea of liberal and socialist interventionism and statism is somehow not patriotic. That, Sir, is just unworthy of response. It is contemptuous of millions and millions of Canadians who have shucked off the idea of statism and intervention and say: "Let us stand on our own two feet in the world" and, yes, in partnership with the United States if we choose but not if we choose not.
Timing to the question having to do with the conduct of this bill through its various stages in our Parliament, I will not go through the history of it again because I have done so already tonight. However, to have it proposed to us that it is a shocking contempt of Parliament to allocate seven hours to third reading of this very significant bill is an unfair accusation. This bill, in the mother of Parliaments, would have had two or three hours maximum, but this is not the mother of Parliaments. This is a Parliament where the opposition has the maximum opportunity to make its point, and I think that nourishes democracy.
I find it rather strange and somehow shocking and disappointing that the hon. member who holds a responsible position within his party and who is something of an expert in the rules of Parliament has abused the terms of an agreement which his party entered into. He is abusing the very terms of an agreement which his party entered into. He suggested that the government has fled because it did not want to hear the arguments of the opposition.
I have already gone on record tonight as having said that I responded to every one of the opposition amendments fully. I explained and defended fully every one of the government amendments in the 11 hours that we spent going through detailed clause by clause study of this bill. Many of those amendments, in fact the vast majority of them, were withdrawn after that agonizing process had been gone through so that they could be reintroduced at report stage to tie up the business of the House further, after the issues had been thoroughly aired.

We have had this described by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands as somehow constituting Tory arrogance, this allocation of so much quite properly to the study of a bill and the opportunity for the opposition to have its views made known on the bill and its provisions.
I knew the Tory great-uncle of this man. He would be spinning in his grave to hear history being rewritten and redescribed as it is being described here today. That distinguished great-uncle of the member for Kingston and the Islands married a lovely lady who remains my constituent in her late nineties. She is the daughter of the founding premier of the province of Alberta, a Liberal premier who later saw the error of his ways and became a distinguished Conservative.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the parliamentary secretary's sentiments in respect of my relatives who live in his riding, but I assure the House that there will be no spinning in any graves except for the misconceptions that the parliamentary secretary is spreading.
Let us turn to one of the points. I do not want to deal with all of them. My arguments stand firmly on their own two feet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: You cannot remember them.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: There is that difficulty, but never mind that. The fact is that the parliamentary secretary suggested in respect of the committee that he spent 11 hours slugging it out, as I admit he did. He worked. There is no question that when the parliamentary secretary is here he works. He worked away in this committee, slugging it out for 11 hours discussing these amendments. That may be so, but the fact is that those hours were spent when the committee was in clause by clause study. From what the hon. member for Mount Royal has indicated to me, that was in closed session.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: No, it was open.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
It was open but, as the hon. member knows, very few people attend those sittings. The committee hearings were not televised. Debate on report stage of this bill was on national television, so Canadians could see what the government was planning to do to the CBC. They could see what the government was planning to do by changing the rules under the Broadcast Act. That was the purpose of bringing the amendments in the House of Commons, so Canadians could see what was going on and make a public display of the despicable way the government is acting in respect of this bill and in
Government Orders
respect of the CBC. That is why it was done this way and surely the parliamentary secretary knows that.
Yet, he says that seven hours of debate on third reading is generous. Rubbish, that is generous. This government, since this Parliament began, has taken it into its head-and the government House leader is largely responsible for this-that it somehow can limit debate to whatever it thinks is appropriate.
We can hear the government House leader say: "I think more than one day on that bill is too long." That is his view, but that is not our view. It was not our view when we were in government.
We gave the hon. members opposite all kinds of time when this party was in government. I have read Hansard where debates went on for weeks and weeks and weeks.
The hon. member for Saint-Denis is here. He can testify as to how many weeks the Conservative Party, when it was in opposition, dragged out debates-weeks and weeks.
The hon. parliamentary secretary thinks that seven hours is excessive. He said they would not allow seven hours in the U.K. Big deal. I do not care whether they allow seven hours in the U.K. As I said, this is not the United Kingdom. This is Canada and the hon. member should learn the difference. He cannot always cite the other for examples of how it works. The United Kingdom's parliament is a unitary parliament. There are no provinces. There is no provincial legislature. It passes all the legislation that we do in all legislatures and here for the whole U.K. It is a different kettle of fish. It is a different ball game and the hon. member should realize that.
The second point I wanted to make was that he suggested that somehow I was critical-I have forgotten his words-and that I did not agree with the agreement we had already agreed to.
I am saying we agreed to it because the choice was to have a two or three hour debate or have one that went on into the night. That is why I criticized it and I was very careful to criticize it on that basis. I am not being critical because we got the time or because we agreed to take the time. I am being critical because what we are doing to get the time is saying: "We will suspend all the normal rules and you guys do not have to stay around and listen. We just want to have our day in court and have our chat."


Government Orders
The attitude of the government is: "As long as you just want to talk, we will let you go. But if we have to sit here and keep order in the House and maintain an interest in the debate, then we do not want any part of it and we will not agree." That is the approach of the government, and I am saying that is a bad approach and it shows arrogance, Tory arrogance, pure and simple. It is arrogant, with respect, Mr. Speaker. It is arrogant.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: For only one minute, the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap.

Mr. Speaker, in listening to the debate tonight and watching the debates with regard to Bill C-40 take place over the last number of months, it is all becoming very clear what the government strategy has been.
We were debating Bill C-40 back in the spring when suddenly it was pulled. It was pulled when the government went into the Meech Lake crisis. I think it was pulled very specifically because the government did not want to be criticized for doing exactly what it is doing, undermining the national unity clause with this legislation.
Suddenly, it went silent and remained silent until the dust settled, until Meech was settled, and until Oka was over. Then, it brought it back in, only to pull it again and to bring it back in a third time. Suddenly, there is such a rush for debate that we had to cram it all into a few days.
The government sat absolutely silent during that debate yesterday. Not even the minister would stand up and defend the amendments and defend the legislation. We got absolute silence. Only tonight did we get the parliamentary secretary commenting, to his credit.
What has been the strategy here? What is the hurry for this sudden rush to put this bill through? It became clear tonight with the recognition of the fact that we have 1,200 people being laid off in the near future with the cuts to CBC, the cuts that had been instituted by the government. That was the strategy. They wanted to ram this legislation through to get it out of the House, to be dispensed with, so that when the cuts came down, when the axe fell, it was already finished.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Thirty seconds, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quite agree with the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap. There was an attempt by the government to hold this legislation back last June when it knew that it would be disruptive to national unity. The parliamentary secretary knows that was the reason it was held up last June.
The attempt was to jam this thing through tonight before these cuts got out. The government knew the cuts were coming. It may be that it was the CBC that did the cuts, not the government, but the only reason the CBC did them was because the government reduced the money it had available. It is as simple as that, and that is what has gone on. For the parliamentary secretary to suggest otherwise is palpable nonsense.
